weeks.title: Pride: Leaving Our Proper Place, Grasping Power
weeks.keyText: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
weeks.theme: Pride is not merely thinking too highly of ourselves; it is leaving our proper place as human beings and reaching for power that belongs to God alone.
group: Read James 4:1-10. Why is the statement “God resists the proud” so serious?
In church, what “spiritual costume” does pride most often wear? Which one have you worn yourself?
This week, in what one matter are you willing to deliberately let go of “my way”? Ask someone in the group to keep watch with you in prayer.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, before you walk into the service, ask the Lord to search you: “Am I here today to worship, or to keep score?” During the service, notice when thoughts of comparison, criticism, or wanting to be seen rise up in your heart, and quietly tell the Lord, “You are Lord; I am your servant.” Afterward, pick one small job nobody is rushing to do, and quietly finish it.

lessons.title: God Resists the Proud
lessons.hear:
James 4 opens with a question no church can escape: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” (James 4:1). His answer isn’t the system, the pastor, or that one difficult co-worker. It’s the desires within us. Then he gives the weightiest line of the whole passage: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

The word “resists” carries the sense of an army drawn up in battle formation against an opponent. God doesn’t say he merely “dislikes” the proud; he says he personally takes his stand on the other side. Why is pride so serious in God’s eyes? Because pride is not a minor character flaw. It is the root of the whole fall. When the serpent tempted Eve, his offer was this: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). Humanity wanted more than a piece of fruit. We wanted God’s place—to decide good and evil for ourselves, to be our own lord and king.

That is how the 321 Vision defines pride: leaving our proper place and grasping power. Our proper place is that of creature, servant, and child; God’s power is to decide right and wrong, to hold the glory, and to determine the outcome. Pride is when I get up from my human place and reach out to sit on God’s throne. It isn’t always loud. Often it is very quiet: I silently rule in my heart on who is spiritual and who isn’t; I insist things must be done my way; I secretly hope to be noticed, thanked, and consulted.

But don’t hear only the judgment; hear the grace as well. Right before that heavy line, James says, “But he gives more grace” (James 4:6). God resists pride because pride will destroy us; he gives grace to the humble because humility makes room for grace to flow in. And the way out is simple: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10). Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you: in my church life, which chair have I been sitting in that doesn’t belong to me?
lessons.light: The self-centered life revolves around itself; it wants to be its own lord and king and to take God’s place. This is not a side issue but the very root of humanity’s fall. The most frightening thing about pride is that it puts God on the opposite side from me. Returning to my proper place is not being demoted; it is coming back to where grace can flow in—letting God be God and letting me be human.
think: In James 4:6-10, how does God respond to the proud, and how does he respond to the humble?
In what recent church matter have I wanted to be the one who decides and calls the shots?
In what one matter can I hand the authority to judge back to God today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you are God, and I am human. I confess that I often quietly leave my human place, wanting to judge people for you, control outcomes for you, and share in the glory that belongs only to you. Shine your light on the hidden pride within me, so that I no longer set myself against you, but humble myself before you and receive your greater grace. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight before bed, take five minutes to write down the church matter where you most want things done “my way.” Beside it write, “Lord, you are Lord,” and entrust it to God in prayer.
lessons.quick: Pride is sitting in God’s chair; humility is returning to my human place.
text: You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”?
But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

lessons.title: Pride in Spiritual Clothing
lessons.hear:
In one church there was a brother who had served for more than twenty years. He was full of zeal: he held the keys, he managed the equipment, and he planned the Sunday order of service. When young newcomers wanted to learn the sound board, he always said, “You’re not familiar with it yet—I’ll handle it.” When the new pastor proposed a few changes, he sat silent in the elders and deacons board meeting, then made several phone calls afterward: “I’m not against the pastor. I just want what’s best for the church.” Little by little, fewer people were willing to serve, and the church grew quieter and quieter.

In his third letter, John mentions a man: “Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say” (3 John 9). Diotrephes was probably no outsider; he was likely an influential figure in that local church. His problem was not that he refused to serve, but that he “loves to be first”—he had to be number one and have the final say. As a result, he slandered the apostles with wicked words, refused to welcome the brothers himself, and even threw out of the church those who did (see 3 John 10).

Many of us hold an old mindset: pride is a problem for show-offs who love the spotlight. I serve so faithfully—how could I be proud? But God’s perspective is this: pride loves to dress up in spiritual clothing. It can be called “responsibility” when it is really refusing to let go. It can be called “a burden from the Lord” when it is really insisting on my way. It can be called “standing for the truth” when it is really not being able to stand someone else being right. It can even be called “humility” when it is really waiting for others to praise how humble I am.

What grieves the heart most about pride in the church is its fruit: it drives people away. Diotrephes drove out brothers. Today’s pride may drive away a young person who wanted to learn to serve, a sister who no longer dares to share her ideas, or a family that quietly moves to another church. John’s appeal is gentle and clear: “Beloved, don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good” (3 John 11). Let the Holy Spirit honestly open up your spiritual clothing: is part of my service actually about protecting my position?
lessons.light: Loving to be first is leaving our proper place and grasping power. In the church, the Lord gives me a post of service, not a piece of territory to own. The test is simple: when someone else can take over, disagree with me, or even do it better than I do, do I feel joy or unease? Where I feel uneasy is often exactly where the self-centered life is hiding.
think: In 3 John 9-11, what behaviors grew out of Diotrephes’ love of being first?
Is there any area of my service where I refuse to let go or fear being replaced?
Which member of the body can I invite to share in the ministry I’m carrying?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the head of the church, and I am only your servant. Uncover the pride in my heart that I have wrapped in spiritual language, and forgive me for treating my service as territory and my co-workers as threats. Make me glad to see others grow, even to surpass me, so that you receive all the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone in your area of ministry who seldom gets a chance to serve. Send a message inviting them to join you next time, and arrange to teach them one thing you know well.
lessons.quick: Pride loves to wear spiritual clothing; only when I take it off do I see that I’ve been protecting myself.
text: I wrote to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say.

Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds which he does, unjustly accusing us with wicked words. Not content with this, he doesn’t receive the brothers himself, and those who would, he forbids and throws out of the assembly.
Beloved, don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good. He who does good is of God. He who does evil hasn’t seen God.

lessons.title: Whoever Would Be Great Must Serve
lessons.hear:
The mother of Zebedee’s sons came with her two boys and knelt before Jesus—but what came out of her mouth was a request about seats: “Command that these, my two sons, may sit, one on your right hand, and one on your left hand, in your Kingdom” (Matthew 20:21). When the other ten disciples heard it, they were indignant. They weren’t upset because they were more humble; they were upset because someone had beaten them to it. That’s how pride always works: when one person reaches for a seat, everyone else is stirred to grab one too.

Jesus didn’t scold them for wanting to be great. Instead, he redefined greatness: “whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant” (Matthew 20:26-27). In the world, greatness is measured by how many people serve me; in God’s kingdom, it is measured by how many people I serve. The world’s road climbs up; the kingdom’s road goes down.

Pride can’t be removed by self-reflection alone. It also takes action in the opposite direction. The hand that grasps for power must learn to let go; the feet that head for the seat of honor must learn to walk toward the lower place. Here are three options for today—just pick one: 1. At a service or small group, do a small job no one will notice or thank you for, such as stacking chairs, washing cups, or taking out the trash, and tell no one afterward. 2. In a setting where you usually take the lead, ask for others’ opinions first and genuinely adopt one of them. 3. Go to a brother or sister you have quietly looked down on and ask them for help with something they’re good at.

Choosing the lower place feels awkward at first, like shoes you haven’t broken in. But after a while you’ll notice a wonderful lightness, because you no longer have to prop up that “important me.” Jesus said, “the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve” (Matthew 20:28). When we follow him downward, we step into his very life.
lessons.light: Humility is not just a feeling; it is a direction. Pride grasps upward; humility lets go downward. “Serve” in the Way of Service means letting Jesus reign and serving in his strength. When I gladly become a servant, I give the place of “first” back to Jesus, and the people around me get to see what he looks like.
think: In Matthew 20:24, why were the other disciples indignant? What does that reveal?
In what settings do I habitually take the best seat or have the last word?
Which “going down” action will I choose today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are Lord, yet you came to serve, and even gave your life for me. I confess that I often want to be served, to be valued, to be invited to the seat of honor. Today give me a servant’s heart. Lead me to do one small, unseen task, and meet me there. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Choose one of the three options today and do it without telling anyone. Tonight, say just one sentence to the Lord: “Lord, I did this for you.”
lessons.quick: The world’s greatness climbs up; the kingdom’s greatness goes down.
text: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, kneeling and asking a certain thing of him.
He said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Command that these, my two sons, may sit, one on your right hand and one on your left hand, in your Kingdom.”

But Jesus answered, “You don’t know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?” They said to him, “We are able.”

He said to them, “You will indeed drink my cup, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with; but to sit on my right hand and on my left hand is not mine to give, but it is for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”
When the ten heard it, they were indignant with the two brothers.
But Jesus summoned them, and said, “You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
It shall not be so among you; but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant,
even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.title: Why Him and Not Me?
lessons.hear:
Miriam was Moses’ older sister. Long ago she had kept watch over baby Moses by the river; after the crossing of the Red Sea, she took up her tambourine and led the women in song. She was someone God used. But one day she and Aaron said, “Has the LORD indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?” (Numbers 12:2). The stated reason was that Moses had married a Cushite woman. The real issue was this: Why him and not us?

Every co-worker in ministry should stop and listen to that sentence. Pride rarely begins by saying, “I want to be king.” It usually says, “God uses me too—why should I have to listen to him?” It starts with comparison, finds its voice in criticism, and ends up challenging the order God himself established. The text slips in a quiet line: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth” (Numbers 12:3). Moses did not defend himself; God himself stepped in and spoke. When the cloud lifted, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow.

This doesn’t mean leaders can never be challenged. Biblical correction is given face to face, in the fear of God, and for God’s purposes. Miriam’s problem was not honest counsel but comparison and criticism behind his back. Today, quietly hold yourself up to this story: when others are praised or given responsibility, does “Why not me?” spring up in my heart first? Have I said things behind someone’s back that I wouldn’t dare say to their face? Have I used “God speaks to me too” as an excuse not to work together with others?

But the story doesn’t end in judgment. Moses pleaded for the sister who had wounded him: “Heal her, God, I beg you!” (Numbers 12:13). Miriam was shut outside the camp for seven days, and the whole people did not move on until she was brought back in (see Numbers 12:15). That is the path of correction: confess, return to your proper place, and be restored—and the community did not leave her behind but waited to journey on together. Pride must be dealt with, but proud people can still be healed.
lessons.light: When we’re out of our proper place, our relationships fall into disorder. Miriam left her place as sister and co-worker and reached for something that belongs to God alone: the right to choose. Correction begins with returning to my proper place—letting God decide whom he uses where, while I simply stay faithful at my own post. This is letting God be God and letting people be people.
think: In Numbers 12:1-10, what were Miriam and Aaron really unhappy about?
About which co-worker have I ever thought, “Why him?”
If I have talked about someone behind their back, how will I set it right today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you search my heart. I confess that I have compared and envied, and have said things behind people’s backs that I should not have said. Heal the leprosy in my heart. Bring me back to the place you have given me, make me faithful at my own post, and help me truly give thanks for the people you are using. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you remember a co-worker you have talked about behind their back, first confess it to the Lord. Then, sometime this week, thank that person face to face for one area of their service, naming specifically the good you’ve seen.
lessons.quick: “Why him?” is where pride begins; “Lord, you are Lord” is where healing begins.
text: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married; for he had married a Cushite woman.
They said, “Has the LORD indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?” And the LORD heard it.
Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.
The LORD spoke suddenly to Moses, to Aaron, and to Miriam, “You three come out to the Tent of Meeting!” The three of them came out.
The LORD came down in a pillar of cloud, and stood at the door of the Tent, and called Aaron and Miriam; and they both came forward.
He said, “Now hear my words. If there is a prophet among you, I, the LORD, will make myself known to him in a vision. I will speak with him in a dream.
My servant Moses is not so. He is faithful in all my house.
With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see the LORD’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
The LORD’s anger burned against them; and he departed.
The cloud departed from over the Tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow. Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous.

lessons.title: Two Men Went Up to Pray
lessons.hear:
This week we have seen pride’s true face. It is not just an arrogant attitude; it is leaving our human place and grasping God’s power, and in church it often dresses up in spiritual clothing. To close the week, let Jesus engrave this truth on our hearts with a parable.

Two men went up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee stood, and every word he said was true: he fasted, he tithed, he didn’t extort or commit adultery. His problem wasn’t his behavior but his position. He had stepped up onto God’s judgment seat to evaluate others and himself: “God, I thank you, that I am not like the rest of men, extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector” (Luke 18:11). The tax collector, meanwhile, stood far off and only beat his breast, saying, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).

Notice that Jesus told this parable “to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others” (Luke 18:9). Trusting in ourselves and looking down on others are the two marks of pride, and they show up most easily in people who already feel at home in church. The Old Testament puts it bluntly: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). Jesus’ conclusion: “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

To repeat means to bring this truth back into daily life again and again: every time your heart says, “I’m not like him,” stop and pray the tax collector’s prayer instead. To multiply means to let this truth flow to others—not by pointing out other people’s pride, but by sharing your own first. When you honestly say, “This week God showed me that I wanted to be in control of such-and-such,” you open a door for someone else to safely return to their proper place too. Humble sharing often draws out a humble response.
lessons.light: Changing a mindset takes repetition until it becomes a new reflex. Pride’s reflex is “I’m not like him”; humility’s reflex is “Lord, have mercy on me.” This is where we practice the “0” of 920: with every “2” in my life, I set myself aside first and let the life of Christ show through.
think: In Luke 18:9-14, how did the “positions” of the Pharisee and the tax collector differ?
How many times this week has my heart said, “I’m not like him”? About whom?
With whom will I share one area of pride that God showed me this week?
lessons.speak: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. I will no longer trust in myself or look down on others. Thank you for showing me this week where I have left my proper place. Bring me back to the tax collector’s place every day, and let my humble sharing become a blessing to others. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, find your spiritual companion or a small group member and take three minutes to share one area of pride God has shown you. Ask them to keep watch over you in prayer for the next month.
lessons.quick: Stop saying “I’m not like him”; just say “Lord, have mercy on me.”
text: He also spoke this parable to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others:
“Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

weeks.title: Humility: Returning to Our Proper Place, Laying Down Power
weeks.keyText: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
weeks.theme: Humility is not thinking little of ourselves; it is returning to our proper place as human beings—letting people be people and God be God.
group: Read Philippians 2:5-11. When Jesus “emptied himself,” what did he lay aside, and what did he take on?
Have you ever mistaken low self-esteem for humility? How do the two look different in everyday life?
This week, whose feet in your small group are you willing to “wash”? Name one specific action.
weeks.sunday: The night before Sunday, slowly read Philippians 2:5-8 and ask the Lord to put the mind of Christ in you. During the service, treat the songs as prayers of surrender rather than a performance to rate, and give thanks for every co-worker serving up front and behind the scenes. Afterward, ask one ministry team member, “Is there anything I can help with?”—and then really stay and help.

lessons.title: He Emptied Himself, Taking the Form of a Servant
lessons.hear:
Last week we looked at pride: leaving our proper place and grasping power. This week we look at humility in its most perfect form. Paul doesn’t begin by defining humility; he points us to a Person: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5).

Notice the direction of this passage. Adam was a man, yet he reached out to be “like God.” Christ was God, yet he “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:6-7). Adam grasped upward; Christ let go downward. Adam seized what wasn’t his and lost everything; Christ laid down what was rightfully his, and God “highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:9). The whole story of salvation in the Bible turns on this one grasping and this one letting go.

“Emptied himself” does not mean Jesus stopped being God. It means he willingly refused to use his rights for his own advantage. He had every right to be served, yet he chose to serve; every right to avoid suffering, yet he chose the cross. This is what the 321 Vision means by humility: laying down power and returning to our proper place. Jesus took the human place, “becoming obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8). For us, humility means being at peace as created human beings, as God’s children, as members of Christ’s body—and giving God’s place back to God.

There is great comfort here. Humility doesn’t make me small; it puts me back where I truly belong. Picture a planet returning to its orbit: no longer careening wildly, it finds stability in the pull of the sun. When I stop straining to be God, I’m free to simply be human; when I let God be God, he does in me what he intends to do. That’s why humility is the key to revival: once the door opens, grace comes in.
lessons.light: Pride says, “I want to be like God.” Christ says, “I am willing to become human.” Letting Jesus reign means having his mind in us—not treating our rights as something to grasp, but counting obedience as glory. Jesus is my example: the downward road he walked is the very road back to my proper place.
think: In Philippians 2:6-8, what steps did Christ take on his way down?
What “right” do I find hardest to let go of—being respected, being heard, or being thanked?
Today, at church or at home, which right can I lay down?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet for my sake you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and even died on the cross. I keep grasping upward, while you kept going down. Put your mind in me, make me willing to return to my proper place, and reign in my life. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, put Philippians 2:5 on your phone’s lock screen or on a sticky note. Each time you see it, ask yourself, “Right now, how would the mind of Christ respond to the person in front of me?”
lessons.quick: Adam grasped upward and lost everything; Christ let go downward and was highly exalted.
text: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.
Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name,
that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth,
and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

lessons.title: Humility Is Not Low Self-Esteem
lessons.hear:
A sister had served in the choir for many years when the choir director asked her to give her solo to a younger singer. Out loud she said, “That’s fine. I don’t sing well anyway—who am I?” But she went home and cried all night, and for the next three months she found excuses to skip rehearsal. She thought she was being humble, but what had actually been wounded was her “self.”

Many of us hold an old mindset: humility means putting yourself down and saying “I can’t” about everything. But low self-esteem and pride are actually twins. Both keep the spotlight on me. One thinks I’m too good; the other thinks I’m too bad. One wants others to look up to me; the other wants others to come and comfort me. God’s perspective is this: humility isn’t thinking little of yourself; it’s thinking of yourself very little.

Paul describes humility this way: “in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:3-4). Counting others better than yourself doesn’t mean pretending you have no gifts. It means putting other people’s good ahead of your own pride. And the strength to do that doesn’t come from putting yourself down; it comes from “any exhortation in Christ, … any consolation of love” (Philippians 2:1). A person who knows they are already loved and accepted in Christ no longer needs a position to prove themselves—and no longer needs to hide in self-pity.

Later, as she prayed, that sister sensed the Lord’s light on her heart: “When you sing, is it for me or for you?” She returned to the choir and offered to rehearse with the young singer, teaching her how to breathe. That Christmas she stood in the second row of the choir and sang with more joy than ever before. She hadn’t become small. She had simply returned to her proper place.
lessons.light: Low self-esteem and pride are both forms of the self-centered life—the focus is still on me. True humility is selflessness: not seeing myself as worthless, but seeing myself the way God sees me, and then turning my eyes toward others. Such a person can receive praise and can also accept being replaced, because their worth has already been settled in Christ.
think: In Philippians 2:1-4, what is the foundation of humility, and how does it show itself?
Am I more prone to pride or to low self-esteem? When did it last show up?
How can I “look to the things of others” this week and concretely help one brother or sister flourish?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that in Christ you already love me and accept me. Forgive me for sometimes exalting myself and sometimes hiding in low self-esteem—both of them centered on me. Make me secure in your love, able to count others better than myself and glad to help them flourish. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, sincerely compliment a brother or sister who is stronger than you in some area, naming one specific thing they do well. If you tend to say “I’m not good enough,” try simply saying “Thank you” and receiving a compliment today.
lessons.quick: Humility isn’t thinking little of yourself; it’s thinking of yourself very little.
text: If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassion,
make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind;
doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

lessons.title: Taking Up the Towel
lessons.hear:
On the night of the Last Supper, someone was missing from the room—the servant who should have taken up the basin and washed everyone’s feet. The disciples filed in one by one, and no one moved. Luke tells us that on that very night they were still arguing about which of them was the greatest (see Luke 22:24). And into that awkward silence, Jesus stood up.

When John records the scene, he begins with a crucial sentence: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God, arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” (John 13:3-4). Notice the order. Jesus knew exactly who he was, where he had come from, and where he was going—and that is why he could bend down. True humility is not the absence of identity; it is an identity so secure that it no longer needs to prove anything.

Washing feet was the lowliest job of the day. Feet were covered with dust and sweat and whatever had been stepped in along the road. Jesus knelt down and washed them all—even the feet of Judas, who was about to betray him. Then he said, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14).

What does “foot washing” look like in today’s church? It’s rolling up your sleeves to face a kitchen piled with dirty dishes after a gathering. It’s going with an elderly member, just home from the hospital, to a follow-up appointment. It’s watching the kids for a night so busy young parents can get a break. It’s offering practical help to a co-worker who once offended you. That last one is the hardest—and the most like Jesus. Today, take up the towel that belongs to you. It doesn’t have to be big, only real; it doesn’t have to be seen, only done for the Lord.
lessons.light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our proper place. Jesus held all things in his hands, yet chose to pick up a towel—the most beautiful picture of “Serve” in the Way of Service: letting Jesus reign and serving people by his life. People matter more than tasks, and the one whose feet most need washing is often the person hardest to get along with.
think: According to John 13:3, what did Jesus “know”? How did that enable him to wash feet?
Is there a “basin no one wants to touch” in my church that I keep pretending not to see?
Whose feet will I “wash” today, and in what concrete way?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are Lord, yet you knelt to wash your disciples’ feet—even the feet of the one who would betray you. Let me know clearly who I am in your love, so that I am free to bend down. Today, lead me to take up the towel and serve the one you want me to serve. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose a brother or sister (ideally someone you find hard to get along with) and do something practical for them—bring a meal, give them a ride, or help with an errand—expecting nothing in return.
lessons.quick: Only someone who knows who they are can bend down to wash another’s feet.
text: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”
Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.”
Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!” Jesus answered him, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.”
For he knew him who would betray him; therefore he said, “You are not all clean.”
So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.

lessons.title: Clothed with Humility
lessons.hear:
The man who wrote “clothe yourselves with humility” was Peter. He probably never forgot that night: the Lord wrapped a towel around his waist and knelt in front of him, and Peter said, “You will never wash my feet!” That same night he boasted, “Even if all will be made to stumble because of you, I will never be made to stumble” (Matthew 26:33). A few hours later, he denied the Lord three times.

Peter’s fall exposed the two faces of pride: refusing to be served, and trusting too much in himself. Later, by the Sea of Galilee, the risen Lord asked him three times whether he loved him (see John 21:15-17)—with no rebuke, only restoration, and he even entrusted his sheep to Peter’s care. Years later, this restored apostle wrote to the churches: “all of you clothe yourselves with humility, and subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5). The word Peter uses for “clothe yourselves” pictures tying on a servant’s apron—it calls to mind the towel the Lord wrapped around his waist. Peter had learned the lesson.

Today, use Peter’s story to examine yourself. First, do I refuse to accept help from others? The self-centered person hates being in anyone’s debt, because accepting help means admitting I have needs. Second, do I trust too much in my own judgment, experience, or spiritual maturity? Third, am I carrying every burden on my own shoulders? Peter goes on: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). There is a reason this sentence sits in a passage about humility: anxiety that refuses to let go is often hidden pride—the assumption that everything depends on my control.

The way to adjust is this: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6). Today, admit your need, accept help once, and hand over one worry. This isn’t weakness. It is returning to your proper place.
lessons.light: Pride has two faces: refusing to be served and trusting too much in myself. Humility has two movements: submitting to one another and casting my worries on God. Letting God be God means no longer carrying burdens only he can carry; letting people be people means admitting that I need God—and that I need my brothers and sisters.
think: In 1 Peter 5:5-7, what concrete actions are linked with humility?
Which is harder for me: accepting help from others, or handing my worries to God?
This week, whose help will I accept, or which worry will I hand over?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you restored Peter after he fell, and you restore me again and again. I confess that I often refuse to be served, trust too much in myself, and cling tightly to my worries. Today I clothe myself with humility and bow under your mighty hand. I cast this burden on you, because you care for me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down a worry you’ve been carrying alone and hand it to God in prayer. Then tell a trusted brother or sister about it honestly and ask them to pray for you.
lessons.quick: Admitting need, accepting help, and handing over worry—this is being clothed with humility.
text: Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,
casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

lessons.title: Humility Is the Key to Revival
lessons.hear:
After Solomon dedicated the temple, God appeared to him at night and spoke words that countless churches have prayed through the centuries: “if my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14).

Notice the first condition for revival. It isn’t strategy, attendance, or a better sound system. It is “humble themselves.” Many people long for their church to experience revival but hope others will change first: the pastor needs more anointing, the ministry team needs more passion, the members need more zeal. But God says “my people, who are called by my name”—and that includes me. Revival doesn’t begin at the pulpit. It begins in every heart willing to return to its proper place.

Why is humility the key? Because God says he dwells “with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble” (Isaiah 57:15). Pride shuts the door, because it says, “I can do it myself.” Humility opens the door, because it says, “Lord, without you I can’t.” Many revivals in church history didn’t begin with spectacular mass rallies, but with a handful of people confessing their sins before God, forgiving one another, and kneeling to pray.

This week we started with Christ’s self-emptying, distinguished humility from low self-esteem, took up the towel, and learned to clothe ourselves with humility. Now it’s time to repeat and to multiply. To repeat means returning to your proper place every morning with one sentence: “Lord, you are God, and I am human.” To multiply means inviting one or two brothers and sisters to pray through this verse together—not for other people’s repentance, but beginning with “our” repentance. When humble people gather, the door to revival opens a crack.
lessons.light: Humility is the key to revival because it puts God back in God’s place. Change starts with me: I don’t wait for others to change first—I humble myself first, pray first, turn first. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: one humble life does more to bring revival than ten new programs.
think: In 2 Chronicles 7:14, what conditions does God set, and what promises does he make?
When I long for revival in my church, do I usually think first about how others should change?
Whom will I invite to join me in humble prayer for our church?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I am one of your people, called by your name. I will no longer wait for others to change first; begin with me. I humble myself before you, seek your face, and turn from my pride and self-righteousness. Hear us, forgive us, and heal our church, so that your kingdom comes among us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite one or two brothers and sisters to set a time (online is fine) to read 2 Chronicles 7:14 together. Each of you first confess your own pride, then pray together for your church for ten minutes.
lessons.quick: Revival doesn’t start at the pulpit; it starts in a heart that returns to its proper place.
text: Then the LORD appeared to Solomon by night, and said to him, “I have heard your prayer, and have chosen this place for myself for a house of sacrifice.
“If I shut up the sky so that there is no rain, or if I command the locust to devour the land, or if I send pestilence among my people,
if my people who are called by my name will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to prayer that is made in this place.
For now I have chosen and made this house holy, that my name may be there forever; and my eyes and my heart will be there perpetually.

weeks.title: Self-Denial and Selflessness: No Longer I
weeks.keyText: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.
weeks.theme: Selflessness doesn’t mean I disappear; it means I step down from the throne and let Christ live out his life in me.
group: Read Galatians 2:19-21. When Paul says “no longer I,” what has he lost, and what has he gained?
What misunderstandings or fears about “denying yourself” have you had? How does God’s word correct them?
This week, which opinion, credit, or position are you willing to let “fall into the earth”? Ask the group to keep watch with you in prayer.
weeks.sunday: Before Sunday, ask the Lord to show you one area where you are still “living for yourself.” During the service, meditate on “who loved me, and gave himself up for me,” and lay that area at the foot of the cross; as you sing, let the lyrics become your surrender. Afterward, do a small thing for a brother or sister—not for yourself, only for the Lord—and don’t let anyone know.

lessons.title: No Longer I, but Christ
lessons.hear:
Galatians 2:20 may be the single verse in the New Testament that best captures the essence of the Christian life: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20).

When Paul says “no longer I,” who is this “I”? It isn’t Paul’s personality, gifts, learning, or passion—he still had all of those, and God used them mightily. What died was the “I” sitting on the throne: the old self that revolves around itself, insists on being its own lord and king, and tries to make itself righteous. The 321 Vision calls this the self-centered life. The self-centered life is like a clenched fist, gripping its reputation, rights, opinions, and achievements so tightly that it can’t receive anything at all.

So selflessness doesn’t mean “nothing.” It doesn’t mean becoming a person with no thoughts, no feelings, who lets everyone push them around. Selflessness is that clenched fist finally opening, so that the life of Christ can flow in. Paul goes on: “That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God” (Galatians 2:20). He was still alive—still eating, working, debating, weeping—but the source of his life had changed, from me to Christ. That’s why we say selflessness is not emptiness; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. The limited “I” steps down, and the infinite Christ reigns within me.

Where does all this begin? With one phrase: “who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20). Selflessness is not achieved by gritting your teeth through spiritual discipline; it happens when you are melted by love. When I see that the Son of God gave himself up for me, the clenched fist slowly opens. So today, don’t start by asking, “How do I become selfless?” Start by quietly reading this line: he loved me; he gave himself up for me.
lessons.light: The self-centered “I” wants to reign; the selfless “I” lets Jesus reign. And only the selfless can be led by the Holy Spirit, be one with others, and overcome the enemy. Change your mindset and you change your life: I am not “an old self trying hard to be better,” but “a new person who has died and risen with Christ.” This is an identity, not merely a goal.
think: In Galatians 2:20, how does Paul describe the life he now lives?
What part of my life is still like a clenched fist, unwilling to let Christ be Lord?
In one specific situation today, how can I let Christ “live in me”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you loved me and gave yourself up for me. I confess that I have been crucified with you; the “I” that sat on the throne no longer has the right to run my life. Live in me. Live out your own life in my words, my reactions, and my service. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, copy out Galatians 2:20 by hand, write your own name next to each “I,” and read it aloud. Then pray ahead of time about something you’ll face today: “Lord, please live this one through me.”
lessons.quick: It’s not me trying hard to live like Christ; it’s Christ living in me.
text: For I through the law died to the law, that I might live to God.

I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.
I don’t reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!”

lessons.title: Is Self-Denial Losing or Gaining?
lessons.hear:
When a new believer in a small group heard about “denying yourself,” it scared him a little: “Does that mean once I believe, I can’t have my own dreams or opinions anymore? That I have to do whatever the church tells me?” A zealous sister had the opposite reaction. She understood self-denial as “never being allowed to say no,” so she took on four ministries at once, burned out body and soul, and grew less and less patient with her family and co-workers.

Both reactions come from the same old mindset: self-denial means loss, means not wanting anything for yourself. But Jesus’ words follow a completely different logic: “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake will save it.” (Luke 9:24). Jesus isn’t asking us to lose; he wants us to gain. Then he asks, “For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses or forfeits his own self?” (Luke 9:25). The person who truly loses himself is the one who clings tightly to himself.

Notice two keys: “for my sake” and “follow me.” Self-denial isn’t denial for its own sake, and it isn’t about satisfying someone’s demands. It is for Jesus and for others, not for myself. So self-denial does not mean letting people push you around. If someone uses “self-denial” as a pretext to control or exploit you, that isn’t the cross—it’s that person’s self-centeredness, and you can and should seek help from a pastor you trust. Biblical self-denial sometimes means learning to say “no”—to your own pride, your anxiety, and your craving to be needed by everyone. That sister later stepped down from two ministries. She said, “I realized that taking on so much wasn’t all for the Lord. Part of it was being afraid of letting people down.”

Jesus said to take up the cross “daily” (see Luke 9:23). Self-denial isn’t one heroic sacrifice; it’s handing the steering wheel from my hands to Jesus in small things, every single day. What I give up isn’t my life—it’s the “me” that keeps making my life narrower and narrower.
lessons.light: The self-centered person thinks clinging to self is safe, yet the tighter they cling, the narrower life becomes; the selfless person lets go of self and steps into the infinite. The direction of self-denial is everything: for Jesus and for others, not for myself—and not to please people. When we discern by the Holy Spirit, self-denial won’t turn into self-exhaustion.
think: In Luke 9:23-25, how does Jesus explain “losing” and “gaining”?
Which is closer to my own fear or misuse of self-denial?
Is there a ministry I need to re-examine with the question, “Is this for the Lord, or because I’m afraid of disappointing people?”
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I have feared that denying myself would leave me with nothing, and I have also turned self-denial into a burden of pleasing people. Help me understand that following you is how I truly gain life. Today I choose to deny myself, take up my cross, and follow you—for you alone, and for the people you love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list all your current ministries and commitments, and beside each one honestly write “for the Lord / for people / for myself.” Pick one to pray over, asking the Lord whether it needs to change.
lessons.quick: Self-denial isn’t losing yourself; it’s losing the “me” that makes life narrow.
text: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.
For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake will save it.
For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses or forfeits his own self?

lessons.title: A Grain of Wheat Falls into the Earth
lessons.hear:
On his way to the cross, Jesus told a parable any farmer would understand: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). A grain of wheat kept in a pretty box can last a long time, but it will always be just one grain. To bear fruit, it has to be buried in the soil, its outer shell has to crack open, and the life inside has to come out.

In church life, what needs to “fall into the earth” usually isn’t anything big. It’s small, very concrete things: an opinion I’m attached to, a bit of credit I’d love to have mentioned, a seat I’ve grown used to, a conviction that “my way is best.” These things aren’t necessarily wrong in themselves, but if I hold them in a tight grip, they can only “remain by itself alone.”

A small group leader once proposed a plan at a ministry team meeting for caring for newcomers, but the team adopted another co-worker’s plan instead. He felt hurt and almost didn’t want to take part. Later, while praying, he remembered this passage. He decided to throw his full support behind the other plan, and even gave his own best ideas to the other co-worker to use. Six months later, that care program had brought several new families into the church. At the sharing night, no one mentioned his name—but he knew in his heart: the grain of wheat had borne fruit.

Today’s practice is to let one grain of wheat fall into the ground. At a ministry team meeting, in your small group, at home, or in an online group chat, find a place where you can “die”: wholeheartedly support someone else’s plan; give the credit to someone else; let another person do the thing you’re best at while you help on the side. Jesus promises, “If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him” (John 12:26). You don’t have to fight for honor yourself; your heavenly Father will see to it personally.
lessons.light: The selfless life usually overcomes the self-centered life not on a big stage, but over a single opinion, a bit of credit, a single seat. People matter more than tasks: letting something get done someone else’s way often builds people up more than doing it my way. A grain of wheat falling into the ground looks like loss, but it is where the “0” of 920 begins to bear the fruit of “9.”
think: In John 12:24-26, how does Jesus describe death and life, losing and gaining?
What is the “grain of wheat” I’m clutching right now?
In what setting today will I let it fall into the earth?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the grain of wheat that fell into the earth and died for me, bearing much fruit. Give me courage to let go of the opinions, credit, and positions I clutch so tightly. Today lead me to “die” in one small thing, so that your life can flow out through me and bear the fruit you desire. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in a group setting (ministry team meeting, small group, or group chat), wholeheartedly support a brother’s or sister’s idea, or publicly give them credit for something—and don’t add your own version afterward.
lessons.quick: Held in the hand, it stays a single grain; fallen into the earth, it bears much fruit.
text: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life.
If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.

lessons.title: Jacob’s Limp
lessons.hear:
From the moment he was born, Jacob’s “hand had hold on Esau’s heel” (Genesis 25:26), and his very name carries the idea of grabbing. He grabbed his brother’s birthright, grabbed his father’s blessing, and grabbed flocks and wealth at his uncle’s house. Jacob wasn’t an unbeliever; he believed God’s promises. He just spent his whole life trying to seize with his own hands what God already intended to give him. That is exactly the self-centered life: even faith becomes a tool for reaching my goals.

Then came that night at the ford of the Jabbok, when “Jacob was left alone” (Genesis 32:24). Ahead of him was Esau, coming with four hundred men; behind him was a past he couldn’t return to. A man came and wrestled with him until daybreak. The man touched the hollow of his thigh, and Jacob was left limping. And in that moment of utter weakness, Jacob’s grabbing changed direction: “I won’t let you go unless you bless me” (Genesis 32:26). He stopped grabbing at people and things, and took hold of God. God gave him a new name: Israel.

Today, hold Jacob’s life up as a mirror. In my church life, what am I grabbing for? Affirmation, a voice in decisions, a particular role, or having others do things my way? Have I also treated God as a tool to accomplish my plans? Paul says that Christ “died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:15). The heart of this review comes down to one question: for whom do I live, and for whom do I serve?

Adjustment often comes with a “touch on the hip”: a failure, a rejection, a season that leaves me powerless. God can use moments like these to help us loosen our grip. From then on Jacob walked with a limp, yet he walked closer to God than ever before. If you are in a night like that, don’t run. Hold on to God as Jacob did: “Lord, I don’t want to grab things in my own strength anymore. Bless me, and change me.”
lessons.light: The self-centered person grabs at people and things—and even grabs at God—to fulfill their own agenda; the selfless person, touched by God on the hip, holds on to God alone from then on. Adjustment isn’t grabbing harder; it’s changing what you hold on to. Shift your perspective from “What can I get?” to “What does the Lord want to gain in me?”
think: In Genesis 32:24-31, at what moment did Jacob’s “grabbing” change direction?
In church, what do I most want to seize with my own hands right now?
If God is touching my “hip” right now, how will I respond to him?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, like Jacob I often try to seize with my own hands what you intend to give me, and I have even treated you as a tool for my own plans. Touch my hip and loosen my grip, so that I hold on to you alone. From now on, I will no longer live for myself, but for the Lord who died and rose again for me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down one thing in church or ministry you’ve “always wanted to get hold of.” Beside it write, “Lord, I let go; I hold on only to you.” Tuck the paper into your Bible and read it once every day this week.
lessons.quick: Loosen the hand that grabs at people and things, and hold on to God alone.
text: Jacob was left alone, and wrestled with a man there until the breaking of the day.
When he saw that he didn’t prevail against him, the man touched the hollow of his thigh, and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh was strained as he wrestled.
The man said, “Let me go, for the day breaks.” Jacob said, “I won’t let you go unless you bless me.”
He said to him, “What is your name?” He said, “Jacob”.
He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
Jacob asked him, “Please tell me your name.” He said, “Why is it that you ask what my name is?” So he blessed him there.
Jacob called the name of the place Peniel; for he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.”
The sun rose on him as he passed over Peniel, and he limped because of his thigh.

lessons.title: He Must Increase, I Must Decrease
lessons.hear:
John the Baptist’s disciples were anxious: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.” (John 3:26). In a world that measures success by numbers and influence, this was bad news. Yet John’s response is astonishing: “Therefore my joy is made full” (John 3:29). Then he spoke words that have become the motto of servants through the ages: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

How could John be so joyful? Because he knew his proper place: “I am not the Christ, … I have been sent before him” (John 3:28). He was the friend of the bridegroom, not the bridegroom. The friend’s greatest joy is not having the bride look at him, but seeing the bride united to the bridegroom. This is the most beautiful picture of selflessness: my success is that people see more and more of Jesus and need me less and less.

This week we’ve learned about “no longer I,” the gain hidden in self-denial, the grain of wheat falling into the ground, and Jacob’s limp. Now it’s time to repeat and to multiply. In church life, John’s words are the touchstone for multiplication: are the people I lead ending up more dependent on me, or more dependent on Jesus? A small group leader whose members can’t function without him is shepherding from the self-centered life. One who brings members to Jesus, even helping them grow to the point of leading others, is multiplying from the selfless life. The greatest joy of spiritual parents is seeing their children walk with God on their own.

Today, find one person and share with them what you’ve received this week about “no longer I.” As you share, keep the focus not on how spiritual you are, but on how Jesus lives in you. Then encourage them to pass it on to the next person. That way, he increases—and all of us are full of joy.
lessons.light: Within 235, the key to the relationship between spiritual parents and children is selflessness: parents don’t want their children attached to themselves, but united to Christ. My decreasing doesn’t mean I vanish; it means I step back into the friend’s place so the Bridegroom can have his bride. Letting Jesus receive all the glory looks like this kind of joy.
think: In John 3:26-30, how does John view his relationship with Jesus?
Is there any part of my ministry where people depend on me more than on Jesus?
With whom will I share what I’ve received this week, and how will I help them pass it on?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you must increase, and I must decrease. Forgive me for wanting people to see me and rely on me. Make me like John, finding my joy in your increase. And let the people I serve and walk alongside know you more and follow you more closely, so that you receive all the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, find someone you mentor or lead, share what Galatians 2:20 means to you, and invite them to share the verse with someone else next week.
lessons.quick: My joy is that people see more and more of Jesus and need me less and less.
text: They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.”
John answered, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.
You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore my joy is made full.
He must increase, but I must decrease.

weeks.title: Humility Inspires Humility: The Secret of Unity
weeks.keyText: being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
weeks.theme: Pride provokes pride and everyone loses; humility inspires humility and everyone wins. Unity begins when I am the first to bow.
group: Read Ephesians 4:1-6. According to Paul, who gives unity? And what is our responsibility?
Have you experienced a moment when “pride provoked pride” or “humility inspired humility”? Please share.
This week, toward which brother or sister are you willing to take the first humble step? Name a specific action.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, as you walk in, look around and remind yourself: “These people and I belong to one body, one Spirit, one hope.” During the service, silently bless a brother or sister with whom you feel distance; afterward, go and greet them, or resolve in your heart to take the first step toward reconciliation this week.

lessons.title: Eager to Keep the Unity
lessons.hear:
Writing from prison, Paul urged the church in Ephesus to live a life worthy of their calling. The first thing he addressed wasn’t an evangelism strategy or a style of worship. It was unity: “with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love, being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:2-3).

Notice two key points. First, it is “the unity of the Spirit.” We don’t manufacture unity through meetings, votes, or reaching consensus; in Christ, unity already exists—“There is one body and one Spirit” (Ephesians 4:4). Second, our responsibility is to be “eager to keep” it. Like peace in a family, it doesn’t need to be bought new, but it does need to be carefully guarded every day. A single cutting remark or one cold look can crack the wall.

So what do we guard it with? The very first words on Paul’s list are “lowliness and humility.” That’s no accident. Unity’s greatest enemy isn’t differing opinions; it’s pride—I have to be right, I have to win, the other person has to back down first. The 321 Vision puts it plainly: pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and both sides win. When two hard stones collide, all you get are sparks. But if one stone is willing to become soil, it can catch the other.

Over the past three weeks we’ve studied pride and humility, self-denial and selflessness. This week we’ll see their most beautiful fruit in church life: unity. Unity doesn’t mean everyone is the same; it means everyone lets Christ reign. When every member steps down from the throne, only One is left on it—and then the body is naturally one. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you: where am I eagerly keeping the unity, and where am I tearing it down without realizing it?
lessons.light: Only the selfless can be one. When self-centered people each want to reign, the throne gets crowded and the church splits; when selfless people let Jesus reign, everyone stands before the same King and naturally becomes one. Unity isn’t the product of consensus; it is the fruit of surrender.
think: In Ephesians 4:2-3, what qualities does Paul use to keep unity?
Which of my recent words or attitudes might have cracked the wall of my church?
How can I keep “the bond of peace” with one brother or sister today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for joining us into one body through the Holy Spirit. Forgive me for so often tearing down the unity you have given because of my own opinions and pride. Make me humble, gentle, and patient in everything, bearing with others in love and eager to keep the unity of the Spirit. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message of thanks or encouragement to a co-worker who often disagrees with you, naming one specific thing you appreciate about them.
lessons.quick: Unity isn’t manufactured; it is kept by humility.
text: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called,
with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling,
one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all.

lessons.title: Pride Provokes Pride
lessons.hear:
After Solomon died, the people came to the new king, Rehoboam, and asked him to lighten their load. The old men’s advice was simple: “If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them with good words, then they will be your servants forever” (1 Kings 12:7). One humble answer could have won a whole nation. But Rehoboam listened to the young men he had grown up with and answered harshly: “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke” (1 Kings 12:14). Ten tribes broke away, and the kingdom was divided from that day on. One proud word provoked the pride of a whole crowd. The king wouldn’t bow, the people wouldn’t bow, and in the end everyone lost. Proverbs had already said it: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1).

Division in the church often begins exactly this way. At one ministry team meeting, the sister in charge of children’s ministry and the brother in charge of facilities got into a dispute over the use of a classroom. The brother said, “The elders and deacons board decided this. We follow the rules.” The sister shot back, “You people have never cared about the children.” Both felt they were serving the Lord, but their words grew harder and harder. Within a few weeks, each side had its supporters, and snide remarks began showing up in the group chat. No one was really discussing the classroom anymore; everyone was protecting their own face.

Many of us hold an old mindset: whoever gives in first loses, and no one will respect me after that. But God’s perspective is this: pride provokes pride, and in the end there are no winners. In God’s kingdom, whoever lets go first wins first. Rehoboam saved face but lost a kingdom. If, in church, we hold on to “I’m right” but lose a brother or sister, what a great loss that is.

In the end, it was the brother who picked up the phone first: “Sister, I spoke too harshly the other day. I’m sorry. The children really do matter—let’s figure this out together.” There was a moment of silence on the other end, and then she began to cry: “I said things that were too harsh too.”
lessons.light: Pride is like an arms race: you raise your voice, I sharpen my tone; you rally one group, I rally another. The only thing that can stop it is for one side to lay down its weapons first. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan—who loves nothing more than watching two people who both claim to serve the Lord refuse to give an inch.
think: In 1 Kings 12:6-14, what is the fundamental difference between the old men’s advice and the young men’s?
In what recent conversation did I answer hard words with hard words?
If I could have that conversation again, what “gentle answer” could I give?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I’m often afraid that giving in first means losing, so I answer hard words with hard words and even rally people to my side. Forgive my pride. Give me a gentle tongue, and make me willing to lose face rather than lose a brother or sister. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think back on a recent unpleasant conversation. Write down one harsh thing you said, and beside it write a gentle answer you could have given instead. If it’s appropriate, find a chance this week to say it to the other person.
lessons.quick: Pride provokes pride and no one wins; whoever lets go first wins first.
text: King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men who had stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, saying, “What counsel do you give me to answer these people?”
They replied, “If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them with good words, then they will be your servants forever.”
But he abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him.
He said to them, “What counsel do you give, that we may answer these people who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Make the yoke that your father put on us lighter’?”

The young men who had grown up with him said to him, “Tell these people who spoke to you, saying, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but make it lighter to us’—tell them, ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.
Now my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, but I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.’”
So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king asked, saying, “Come to me again the third day.”
The king answered the people roughly, and abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him,

and spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”

lessons.title: Seven Bows and a Running Embrace
lessons.hear:
Twenty years earlier, Jacob had cheated his brother out of their father’s blessing, and Esau had wanted to kill him. Now Jacob was bringing his family home, and he heard that Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men. The night before, he had wrestled with God at the ford of the Jabbok, and he was still limping. Today he would face the person he had wronged most deeply.

Jacob didn’t send men out to fight, and he didn’t prepare a defense. He walked out in front of his whole family, and “bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother” (Genesis 33:3). That was an extremely humble gesture, like a subject approaching a king. The Jacob who had spent his whole life grabbing and trying to stay on top now willingly lay face down on the ground. And then something wonderful happened: “Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept” (Genesis 33:4).

This is humility inspiring humility. Jacob’s bowing didn’t bring revenge; instead it awakened Esau’s tenderness. Pride provokes pride, but humility is contagious too. Jacob even said, “I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God” (Genesis 33:10). A man who had been touched by God saw God in his brother’s face.

Today, think of a brother or sister with whom there’s distance between you, and take the first humble step toward them. Choose one of three: 1. Apologize for your part of the wrong—no “but” attached. 2. Write a card or give a small gift to show you value the relationship. 3. Invite them for coffee and listen first, without rushing to explain yourself. You can’t control whether the other person will “run to embrace you,” but you can decide to bow first.

One caution: if the past hurt involved violence, abuse of power, or anything that makes you feel unsafe, humility does not mean exposing yourself to danger again. Please first seek help from a pastor you trust or a professional, and pursue reconciliation in a safe way.
lessons.light: Humility inspires humility, and both sides win. I bow first not because I’m entirely in the wrong, but because God has already won me, so I no longer need to win. Relationships have an order—first with God, then with people: Jacob met God face to face at the ford before he could meet his brother face to face the next day.
think: In Genesis 33:1-4, how did Jacob approach Esau, and how did Esau respond?
With which brother or sister do I still have unresolved distance?
What first humble step will I take toward them today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for first reaching out your hand of reconciliation to me on the cross. As I think of the brother or sister I’m distant from, give me courage to bow first, apologize first, and bless first, without demanding an immediate response. May my humility draw out humility, so that your family is healed. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, after praying for the brother or sister you’re distant from, choose one of the three options and do it. If the time isn’t right yet, at least write down the first sentence you want to say to them.
lessons.quick: I bow first, not because I’ve lost, but because God has already won me.
text: Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau was coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children between Leah, Rachel, and the two servants.
He put the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear.
He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
He lifted up his eyes, and saw the women and the children; and said, “Who are these with you?” He said, “The children whom God has graciously given your servant.”
Then the servants came near with their children, and they bowed themselves.
Leah also and her children came near, and bowed themselves. After them, Joseph came near with Rachel, and they bowed themselves.
Esau said, “What do you mean by all this company which I met?” Jacob said, “To find favor in the sight of my lord.”
Esau said, “I have enough, my brother; let that which you have be yours.”
Jacob said, “Please, no, if I have now found favor in your sight, then receive my present at my hand, because I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me.

lessons.title: The Lord’s Prayer for Unity
lessons.hear:
On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed for his disciples—and for us: “Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one” (John 17:20-21). In his final hours before the cross, what weighed on the Lord’s heart was whether the future church would be one. He even said that unity is the witness through which the world comes to know him: “that the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17:21).

That should stop us and make us examine ourselves. If the Lord values unity this much, am I a bridge of unity in my church, or a crack of division? Hold yourself up honestly to these questions: Do I like passing stories along? Have I formed a little clique in a private group chat? Do I keep certain people permanently at a polite distance? When a disagreement comes up, do I quietly drop out of that ministry?

Paul and Barnabas were the best ministry partnership in the early church, yet over whether to take Mark along, “the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other” (Acts 15:39). Even spiritual people like them parted ways. But the story didn’t end there. Years later, in his final letter, Paul wrote, “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). The young man he had once refused became his helper in his last years. Scripture doesn’t tell us exactly what happened in between, but we do know this: separation isn’t the end, and correction is possible.

The first step in adjusting is to put yourself back inside the Lord’s prayer: “Lord, you prayed for our unity, but I keep tearing it down.” The second step is to find one specific crack and repair it. Maybe it’s a long-overdue phone call. Maybe it’s no longer forwarding a message that hurts someone. Maybe it’s simply sitting next to that person at the next gathering. Sometimes opinions genuinely differ, and you can divide the work and serve separately—but don’t let your hearts divide. If our hearts are joined in the Lord, the body is still one.
lessons.light: Unity requires everyone to return to their proper place: Christ is the head, and I am a member. The root of division is often the self-centered life—my views, my circle, my hurt. Adjustment doesn’t mean pretending nothing happened; it means letting Jesus reign again. People matter more than tasks: our opinions may differ, but our hearts need not divide.
think: In John 17:20-23, what witness does Jesus say unity will bring?
In my church, am I more of a bridge, or have I unintentionally become a crack?
What specific crack can I repair this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, before your suffering you prayed for our unity, yet I have often torn down your body for the sake of my own pride. Forgive me for the times I have passed along gossip, formed cliques, and quietly withdrawn. Make me a bridge, and give me courage to repair one crack, so that the world may know you through our unity. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify one crack in your church that you helped create (a forwarded message, a season of coldness, a little clique), and do something concrete to repair it: delete, apologize, check in, or invite.
lessons.quick: Our opinions may part ways, but our hearts need not; separation isn’t the end.
text: “Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word,
that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
The glory which you have given me, I have given to them, that they may be one, even as we are one,
I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, that the world may know that you sent me and loved them, even as you loved me.

lessons.title: Oil Running Down from the Head
lessons.hear:
Over these four weeks, we have traveled from pride to humility, from self-denial to selflessness, and finally to unity. Psalm 133 is a song pilgrims sang on their way up to Jerusalem: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1).

The psalmist uses two pictures. The first is oil: “It is like the precious oil on the head, that ran down on the beard, even Aaron’s beard; that came down on the edge of his robes” (Psalm 133:2).
