The oil flows from the head downward—from the high priest’s head all the way to the bottom edge of his robes. Today our High Priest is Christ, and he is the head. When we all place ourselves under him and let him reign, his life flows to every corner of the body. Notice that oil always flows downward. Grace doesn’t climb to high places; it flows to low ones. Where there is humility, there the anointing gathers.

The second picture is dew: like the dew of Mount Hermon coming down on the hills of Zion. Unity isn’t manufactured with noise and fuss; like dew, it settles quietly and refreshes dry ground. The psalmist concludes, “for there the LORD gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (Psalm 133:3). God has appointed his blessing to rest where brothers and sisters live together in unity.

To repeat means condensing these four weeks of lessons into one daily habit: in every interaction, first ask, “Am I in my proper place?” To multiply means letting humility flow downward like the oil. Paul urges us, “Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God” (Romans 15:7). This week, you can lead a companion or your small group in practicing this together: each person names one area where they need to return to their proper place, and then you bless one another. One humble person can move a small group; one united small group can influence a whole church. This is what revival looks like.
lessons.light: Humility inspires humility, like oil flowing downward: from Christ to me, from me to my “2,” and on to the whole body. The relationships of 235—spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, and comrades-in-arms—are all built on this downward-flowing life. Unity lets Jesus receive all the glory.
think: What two pictures does Psalm 133 use to describe brothers living in unity? What does each one mean?
Over these four weeks, what self-centeredness has God shown me most clearly?
How will I lead a companion or my small group in practicing humility together?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are our High Priest and the head of the church. Let your anointing oil flow down from you to me, and to our whole church. Help us live together in unity and accept one another, just as you have accepted us. May the blessing the LORD has commanded rest among us, so that you receive all the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, when you meet with your small group or a companion, have each person name one area where they need to return to their proper place. Then pair up to bless each other and pray together.
lessons.quick: Grace flows down like oil; where there is humility, there blessing gathers.
text: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!
It is like the precious oil on the head, that ran down on the beard, even Aaron’s beard, that came down on the edge of his robes,
like the dew of Hermon, that comes down on the hills of Zion; for there the LORD gives the blessing, even life forever more.

weeks.title: Love: Love Is Patient
weeks.keyText: Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,
weeks.theme: Without love, even the greatest gifts are only a clanging cymbal; with love, the smallest act of service carries the fragrance of Christ.
group: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4-7, replacing “love” first with “Jesus” and then with “I.” How does that make you feel?
What kind of person do you find hardest to love at church? How is God’s love pushing past your boundaries?
This week, for which member of the body (a newcomer, an older saint, or a co-worker) could our small group do one act of love together?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, before you walk into the sanctuary, quietly repeat to yourself: “Love is patient and is kind” (1 Corinthians 13:4). During the service, notice one brother or sister you seldom interact with—maybe even someone you don’t much like—and silently pray one sentence of blessing over them. Afterward, go and greet them, or help them with some small task. Let love begin with a glance and a word of welcome.

lessons.title: Without Love, I Am Nothing
lessons.hear:
The church in Corinth was rich in gifts. Some spoke in tongues, some prophesied, some had deep knowledge, and their meetings were full of energy. Yet it was also a church split into factions, its members constantly trying to outdo one another. Between chapters 12 and 14, where Paul discusses spiritual gifts, he deliberately places chapter 13. It is as if, in the middle of a heated ministry team meeting, he suddenly hits the pause button and says, “I show a most excellent way to you” (see 1 Corinthians 12:31).

Three times Paul says, “but don’t have love.” “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1). Tongues and eloquent speech belong to the stage of worship; prophecy, knowledge, and faith belong to the pulpit and the Bible study; giving to the poor and self-sacrifice belong to the stage of service and generosity. Put it in today’s language: however moving the choir, however profound the sermon, however hard the ministry team works, without love it is only noise in God’s sight, not life.

Then Paul paints a portrait of love: “Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud” (1 Corinthians 13:4). Someone once said that if you replace “love” in this passage with “Jesus,” every line fits perfectly; replace it with “I,” and you can hardly read it aloud. That is exactly the point. This passage is not a moral checklist; it is a portrait of Christ.

That is why the first fruit the Holy Spirit produces is love (see Galatians 5:22). Fruit isn’t glued on from the outside; it grows out of life within. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine His light on you: I make plenty of sound at church—but do I have love?
lessons.light: In 920, the “9”—the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit—begins with love. Love isn’t one more gift; it is the soil in which every gift grows. Self-centered service craves to be seen, so it easily becomes a clanging cymbal. Selfless service lets the love of Christ flow through, so it builds people up. Change begins with our mindset: what matters most about me at church is not how much I have done, but how much I have loved.
think: In 1 Corinthians 13:1-3, what situations does Paul describe as “without love”?
Which of my ministries at church is most likely to turn into a “clanging cymbal”?
In which setting of service today can I deliberately bring love with me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are love itself. I confess that at church I am often busy making noise and forget to love. Holy Spirit, pour the love of God into my heart, so that my words, my songs, and my service all flow out of love, and people see You in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, quietly read 1 Corinthians 13:4-7, slowly replacing “love” with your own name. Circle the line you can hardly bring yourself to read, tell the Lord about it, and ask Him to change you in that very area.
lessons.quick: Without love, everything is a clanging cymbal; with love, even small things become life.
text: If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal.
If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.
If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.
Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,
doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;
doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;
bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.

lessons.title: Love Is from God, Not a Feeling
lessons.hear:
A sister who led the children’s Sunday school kept clashing with the brother who managed the church facilities. The classroom air conditioning wasn’t on, the tables and chairs had been moved, the room booking had been changed. One evening after a ministry team meeting, eyes red, she told her small group leader, “I love the Lord, but I just can’t bring myself to like him.”

Many of us carry an old mindset: love means liking someone; love requires feelings; and the other person has to deserve it. By that standard, there are very few people at church we can love—those we get along with, those who speak kindly, those who are on our side. But John says, “Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God” (1 John 4:7). The source of love is not the feelings in my heart; it is God.

God has never loved us because we were lovable. Moses told Israel, “The LORD didn’t set his love on you nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people” (Deuteronomy 7:7). The New Testament says it even more plainly: “In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4:10). Because God first loved me when I was undeserving, I now have the power to love people who are hard to love.

That sister began praying for the brother, and only then did she learn that every Sunday he arrived two hours before anyone else to unlock the doors, turn on the air conditioning, and set out the chairs—and had done so faithfully for twenty years, rarely hearing a word of thanks. She still didn’t like everything about the way he did things, but she began to seek his good, and at the next ministry team meeting she publicly thanked him for the first time. In that moment, the whole atmosphere of the meeting changed.

Love is a choice—and even more, it is a life. When God lives in us, His love is perfected in us.
lessons.light: The “2” in 920 reminds me that the co-worker I don’t like is also a “2” whom God has placed beside me. Self-centered love only loves those who respond to me; selfless love lets God’s love pass through me to others. The order of relationships is God first, then people: the more I am filled with God’s love, the more I can love those who are hard to love.
think: According to 1 John 4:7-12, where does love come from, and how was God’s love revealed?
Have I been equating “love” with “liking”? Which people has that caused me to miss?
For which hard-to-love brother or sister can I begin praying every day this week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for loving me first, when I was not lovable at all. I confess that I only want to love people who make me comfortable. Put Your love in my heart, so that I can love that brother or sister I find so hard to like, and seek their good. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down the name of the person at church you find hardest to like. Today, pray three blessings over them, and think of one thing you can genuinely thank them for. Write it down and be ready to say it when the chance comes.
lessons.quick: I love not because others are lovable, but because God first loved me.
text: Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.
He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.
By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his only born Son into the world that we might live through him.
In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.
No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.

lessons.title: Loving in Deed and Truth
lessons.hear:
“We’re a very loving church” is how almost every church describes itself. But newcomers often feel differently. When the Sunday service ends, the regulars gather in little circles to chat, while the newcomer stands in a corner scrolling on their phone and, ten minutes later, quietly slips out. The longtime members aren’t cold; they simply didn’t notice.

John brings love back down to earth: “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John 3:16). Laying down our lives sounds far away, but John immediately makes it concrete with something very ordinary: when you see a brother in need, don’t close your heart of compassion. Then he says, “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18).

In church life, acts of love are often small but very real ways of laying ourselves down:
1. Laying down our time: stay ten minutes longer after the service and walk over to the person standing in the corner.
2. Laying down our comfort: sit next to someone from a different generation—listen to an older believer tell the story of their faith when they were young, or teach an elderly saint how to join an online meeting.
3. Laying down our pride: go to the brother or sister you had a small friction with at the last choir rehearsal and say, “Thanks for serving alongside me today.”

Love doesn’t need to wait for the feelings to arrive. Often, the feelings follow after we act. What newcomers remember is often not the content of the sermon, but whether anyone called them by name. Choose one of these today. Don’t advertise it, don’t keep score; just do it for the Lord.
lessons.light: “Laying down our lives for the brothers” is the most everyday form of the selfless “0”: setting aside our time, our comfort, and our pride. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. A church where we let Jesus reign doesn’t prove its love with slogans; its love is seen in countless small acts of self-denial.
think: How does 1 John 3:16-18 bring “laying down our lives” into everyday life?
Does my love at church stay mostly in words, or does it show up in deeds?
Toward which brother or sister will I take one concrete act of love today, and what will it be?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You laid down Your life for me, and that is how I know what love is. Don’t let my love stop at my lips; let it show up in my actions. Open my eyes today to see the brother or sister who is overlooked, and give me courage to lay down my time, my comfort, and my pride to love them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today or this Sunday, pick one newcomer or an older saint who receives little attention. Go and greet them, and remember their name. If possible, invite them to share a meal, or arrange to meet again next week.
lessons.quick: Love is not just on our lips, but in deed and in truth.
text: By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?
My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.

lessons.title: Do You Love Me?
lessons.hear:
Peter once declared with great confidence, “Even if all will be made to stumble because of you, I will never be made to stumble” (Matthew 26:33). It was a sincere love, but a self-centered one—fueled by his own zeal, measured against others, confident in his own ability. That very night, he denied the Lord three times.

The risen Lord did not scold him. Instead, He prepared breakfast on the shore of the Sea of Galilee and then asked him three times, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” (John 21:16). Peter no longer dared to claim he loved Him “more than these.” He only answered, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you” (John 21:16). From a love that boasted to a love that rested in being known by the Lord—this was the turning point of Peter’s life. And every time, the Lord’s response was a commission: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:15). The evidence of loving the Lord is loving His sheep—loving the real people in His church.

Today, use 1 Corinthians 13 as a mirror and review yourself honestly. Do I only love the people who affirm me and respond to me? In my service, do I keep a record of wrongs—remembering who didn’t show up to help last time, who said what in the group chat? When someone else’s service is praised more than mine, can I genuinely rejoice?

After this review, the path of adjustment is not “I must try harder to love.” That would only lead us back down Peter’s old road. The path of adjustment is to return first to the Lord’s love: “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Let the Lord ask you once more, love you once more, and then you will have the strength to turn and feed His sheep.
lessons.light: Peter’s failure was self-centered love hitting a wall; Peter’s restoration was being won over again by the Lord’s love. Selfless love is not “I’m good at loving,” but “the Lord knows me.” Pride says, “I love the Lord more than others do.” Humility says, “Lord, you know.” Loving the Lord takes concrete shape in loving His sheep.
think: After asking Peter three times, what did Jesus entrust to him?
Where is my love like Peter’s—full of self-confidence and comparison?
Having returned to the Lord’s love first, which of His lambs will I go and “feed”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You know everything. You know that I love You, and You know how limited my love is. Forgive me for so often loving my own ministry more than Your sheep. Win me over once more with Your love, and send me out to feed and support the brothers and sisters You have placed beside me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, review your week line by line using 1 Corinthians 13:4-7. Write down one moment when you were “without love” and confess it to the Lord. If it involved a particular brother or sister, reach out to them tomorrow with a kind word or an apology.
lessons.quick: The Lord doesn’t ask how much I’ve done, but: “Do you love me?”
text: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

lessons.title: Love Never Fails
lessons.hear:
So much in church life will pass away. The style of our services will change, new songs will replace old ones, ministry teams will rotate, and even the most outstanding preaching gift will one day fall silent. Paul says, “Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with” (1 Corinthians 13:8). In the end, “now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

The Old Testament tells of a beautiful friendship. Jonathan was Saul’s eldest son, heir to the throne, yet David was the one God had chosen as the next king. By ordinary logic, Jonathan had every reason to be jealous. But Scripture says, “Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:1). When David was being hunted and hiding in the wilderness, Jonathan went to find him in person and “strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16). This was a love that did not seek its own way—a love willing to let someone else rise.

The passing of the baton between generations in the church needs exactly this kind of love: older co-workers willing to help younger ones step up, and younger ones willing to honor the foundations their elders laid; longtime members willing to make room for newcomers, and newcomers treasuring what those before them have given. Love is the power that keeps the body united even as new blood comes in.

Don’t keep this week’s truth to yourself. Multiplication doesn’t mean preaching a sermon; it means telling one person your own experience of being loved: “This week I realized that I can love because God first loved me.” Then, like Jonathan, go and strengthen someone.
lessons.light: The final step in changing a mindset is multiplication. If love stops with me, it remains a nice feeling; only when it flows out does it become life. In 235, spiritual companions and spiritual parents and children are all built on selfless love. Jonathan’s love was the kind that gladly lets others flourish while stepping back himself.
think: According to 1 Corinthians 13:8-13, what will cease, and what will remain?
How has my understanding of “love” changed this week?
Like Jonathan, which brother or sister will I go and strengthen?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for loving me with a love that never fails. Let this love take root in my heart and flow through me to others. Make me like Jonathan—free from envy, not fighting for position, gladly helping others rise—so that Your church is built up in love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find your spiritual companion or a believer younger than you. Spend ten minutes sharing the verse that touched you most this week, and pray for them, asking that their hand would be strengthened in God.
lessons.quick: Everything else will pass away; only love never fails.
text: Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.
For we know in part and we prophesy in part;
but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with.
When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child. Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known.
But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love.

weeks.title: Joy: Rejoicing Together in the Lord
weeks.keyText: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
weeks.theme: Joy rests on the Lord, not on circumstances; rejoicing sincerely when others are blessed is the mark of a selfless life.
group: Paul wrote “Rejoice in the Lord always” from prison. What weight do those words carry given his situation?
At church, which is harder for you: “Rejoice with those who rejoice” or “Weep with those who weep”? Why?
This week, whose good news could our small group celebrate together, or whose restoration could we rejoice over? What exactly will we do?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, before entering the sanctuary, count three graces God has given you this week, and take your seat with thanksgiving. During the service, if anyone shares a testimony, is baptized, or is sent out, rejoice with them wholeheartedly. Afterward, find a brother or sister who has had good news this week and tell them in person, “I’m so happy for you—praise the Lord!”

lessons.title: Rejoice in the Lord Always
lessons.hear:
Philippians is often called “the epistle of joy,” yet its author was a prisoner with an uncertain future, and the church receiving it was not free of problems. Just two verses before this week’s passage, Paul names two women who had labored with him in the gospel and urges them “to think the same way in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). In that setting Paul writes, “Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, ‘Rejoice!’” (Philippians 4:4).

Notice the words “in the Lord.” The world’s happiness depends on circumstances: when things go smoothly, when we are affirmed, when the meeting is full, we are glad; otherwise we are discouraged. But the joy that the Holy Spirit produces has a root that cannot be shaken—the Lord Himself. That is why Paul could rejoice in prison: the Lord was not locked up.

The Old Testament prophet Habakkuk had the same perspective. Facing a bleak scene—fig trees that did not blossom, sheep pens with no flock—he still said, “yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!” (Habakkuk 3:18). That word “yet” is the great divide of joy.

In church life, this joy grows into several shapes. “Let your gentleness be known to all men” (Philippians 4:5): joyful people don’t need to win every argument. “In nothing be anxious” (Philippians 4:6): joyful people hand their burdens to God instead of dumping their anxiety on their co-workers. And the peace of God guards our hearts and minds.

The atmosphere of a church is usually formed by the hearts of its members, one by one. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to root your joy in the Lord once again—not in how the church is performing or in how others treat you.
lessons.light: Keep the focus on Jesus—not on yourself, not on others, not on circumstances. For the self-centered, joy is held hostage by circumstances; for the selfless, joy is rooted in Christ. Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart rather than on yourself with your head: lead with the heart and you find gladness; lead with the head and you find worry. When the Holy Spirit dwells in the heart, joy wells up from within.
think: In Philippians 4:4-7, how is joy connected with gentleness, prayer, and peace?
What has recently stolen my joy at church?
Which worry can I hand over to God today, and receive joy in exchange?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are the source of my joy. I confess that I often let circumstances, other people’s attitudes, and the success or failure of my ministry rule my moods. Today I hand my worries to You. Holy Spirit, help me rejoice in the Lord always, and let my joy be a blessing to the church. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down one thing that has robbed you of joy at church. Pray about it the way Philippians 4:6 describes: first bring your request, then write down three things about it you can thank God for.
lessons.quick: Circumstances change, but the Lord does not; I rejoice in Him always.
text: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.title: Heaven Rejoices—Does the Church?
lessons.hear:
A young man who had wandered for years came back to church. In the past he had broken his parents’ hearts and caused no small amount of trouble at church. This Sunday he stood at the front to share his testimony of how the Lord had brought him back. Some in the congregation wiped away tears; a few longtime members muttered, “Let’s see how long this lasts.”

Many of us hide an old mindset in our hearts: joy depends on whether someone “deserves” it. When a diligent person is recognized, we are glad; but when a prodigal returns, or a latecomer receives the same grace, something in us feels it isn’t fair. That is exactly the attitude of the older brother in Luke 15, who complained to his father, “These many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours” (Luke 15:29), and refused to go in and celebrate.

Jesus told the parables of the lost sheep and the lost coin precisely to change this mindset. When the shepherd finds his sheep, he calls his friends and neighbors together, saying, “Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!” (Luke 15:6). Then Jesus pulls back the curtain on heaven’s heart: “there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7). Heaven’s joy isn’t calculated by merit; it overflows by grace.

Back to that Sunday. After the service, a grandmother in her eighties slowly made her way to the young man, took his hand, and said, “Son, I’ve prayed for you for over ten years, and today the Lord answered.” In that moment, the church caught up with the joy of heaven.

God’s perspective is simple: what makes the Father glad should make me glad; those the Father welcomes, I should welcome too.
lessons.light: Envying someone else’s blessing is the self-centered life keeping accounts; rejoicing over someone else’s blessing is the selfless life at worship. Pride wants God to distribute grace by my standards; humility lets God be God. The “2” in 920 includes that “latecomer” too—a child the Father has brought home, and my own brother.
think: In Luke 15:3-10, what did the owners do after finding what was lost?
Do I have the older brother’s attitude, feeling that someone else’s blessing is “unfair”?
How can I take the initiative to welcome someone who has recently returned to church or newly come to faith?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You that You once brought me home just like this. Forgive the score-keeping and coldness in my heart, and the way I measure other people’s blessings by my own standards. Let my heart keep pace with the joy of heaven, so that I rejoice sincerely over every person who turns back, and welcome them with open arms. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a brother or sister who was recently baptized, made a decision for Christ, or returned to church. Send them a message, or tell them in person on Sunday: “Welcome home—we’re rejoicing over you.”
lessons.quick: What makes the Father glad makes me glad; whom the Father welcomes, I welcome.
text: He told them this parable:
“Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?
When he has found it, he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!’
I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.
“Or what woman, if she had ten drachma coins, if she lost one drachma coin, wouldn’t light a lamp, sweep the house, and seek diligently until she found it?
When she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma which I had lost!’
Even so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner repenting.”

lessons.title: Rejoice with Those Who Rejoice
lessons.hear:
The choir needed to choose a sister to sing the Easter solo. A veteran member who had sung for fifteen years fully expected it to be her—but the director chose a young woman who had joined only a year earlier. She kept coming to rehearsals as usual, but she couldn’t manage a smile. At home she told her husband, “It’s not that I want to compete. I’m just a little hurt.”

Paul says, “Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Many of us discover that weeping together is easier than rejoicing together. When others suffer, our compassion is quickly stirred; when others are honored, comparison often rises in our hearts: why them and not me? Rejoicing with others is hard because it requires selflessness.

The surrounding verses show us how to practice it: “In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another” (Romans 12:10). And again: “Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble” (Romans 12:16). Rejoicing with others doesn’t mean pretending to be happy. It means admitting our disappointment before the Lord, and then choosing to stand on our brother’s or sister’s side.

That veteran singer eventually brought her disappointment to the Lord in prayer. Before the Easter solo, she walked over to the young woman, straightened her collar, and said, “Sing with confidence. I’ll be right behind you, praying for you.” The young woman’s eyes filled with tears. That day, a hymn was sung on the platform—and the gospel was lived out in the pews.

Today, go and do one act of “rejoicing with.” Find a brother or sister who has recently been honored, promoted, chosen, had a baby, or been accepted into school, and celebrate with them from your heart.
lessons.light: Humility inspires humility, and joy inspires joy. When I rejoice in someone else’s success, I am living out “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” The church is no longer a competition but a body—when one member is honored, all the members rejoice together. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.
think: Which phrases in Romans 12:9-16 help us learn to “rejoice with” others?
Has anyone’s recent success stirred up comparison or bitterness in my heart?
Whose good news will I sincerely congratulate today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You know the comparison and disappointment in my heart. I place them in Your hands. Give me a selfless heart that can rejoice sincerely when my brothers and sisters are blessed—without envy, without coldness—so that Your body experiences shared joy through me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find a brother or sister who has recently had good news or been recognized. Call them or write them a card to congratulate them, say specifically what you are rejoicing over, and pray for them.
lessons.quick: Weeping with others takes love; rejoicing with others takes selflessness.
text: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,
not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,
rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer,
contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.
Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse.
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.
Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.

lessons.title: Is It Right to Be Angry?
lessons.hear:
Jonah is the unhappiest preacher in the Bible. His message brought an entire city to repentance. Anyone else would have been leaping for joy, but “it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry” (Jonah 4:1). The reason was simple: he knew that God is “a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger” (Jonah 4:2), and he did not want God to show grace to people he despised.

Even more ironic, when a vine grew up to give him shade, Jonah “was exceedingly glad”; when the vine withered, he was so angry he asked to die. His joy and his anger revolved entirely around himself: my comfort, my opinions, my reputation. God gently asked him, “Is it right for you to be angry?” (Jonah 4:4).

Today, review honestly: in church life, what most often steals my joy? Is it that someone else gets more attention than I do? That decisions don’t go my way? That God uses the very person I dislike? If my joy keeps rising and falling over some “vine,” it shows that my heart is still centered on myself.

The book of Jonah never records his answer, as if leaving the question for every reader. For the path of adjustment, we can learn from John the Baptist. When people told him the crowds were all going after Jesus, he said, “the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore my joy is made full. He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:29-30). His joy didn’t depend on his own platform, but on the bridegroom’s increase.

When Jesus becomes the focus, my joy is set free.
lessons.light: The self-centered need joy to revolve around themselves; the selfless let their joy follow Jesus. Jonah grabbed the power of judgment and tried to decide for God who deserved grace—that is leaving our proper place and grasping power. When I return to my proper place and let God be God, I can say with John, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).
think: Why was Jonah angry, and how did God respond to him?
Which “vine” most often pulls my joy up and down?
In what area am I willing to learn “He must increase, but I must decrease”?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, forgive me for being like Jonah—so often glad about my own comfort, yet displeased when You show grace to others. Remove the envy and score-keeping from my heart. Bring me back to my proper place, let Your joy be my joy, and let Jesus increase while I gladly decrease. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, write down one thing at church that has “displeased” you. Beside it, write the question God might ask you: “Is it right for you to be angry?” Answer honestly, and entrust it to the Lord.
lessons.quick: He must increase, I must decrease—and then my joy is made full.
text: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry.

He prayed to the LORD, and said, “Please, LORD, wasn’t this what I said when I was still in my own country? Therefore I hurried to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and you relent of doing harm.
Therefore now, LORD, take, I beg you, my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”
The LORD said, “Is it right for you to be angry?”
Then Jonah went out of the city and sat on the east side of the city, and there made himself a booth and sat under it in the shade, until he might see what would become of the city.
The LORD God prepared a vine and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head to deliver him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the vine.
But God prepared a worm at dawn the next day, and it chewed on the vine so that it withered.

When the sun arose, God prepared a sultry east wind; and the sun beat on Jonah’s head, so that he was faint and requested for himself that he might die. He said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”
God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the vine?” He said, “I am right to be angry, even to death.”
The LORD said, “You have been concerned for the vine, for which you have not labored, neither made it grow; which came up in a night and perished in a night.

Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who can’t discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also many animals?”

lessons.title: Praying for You with Joy
lessons.hear:
Paul’s opening words to the Philippian church are a joyful thanksgiving: “I thank my God whenever I remember you, always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy” (Philippians 1:3-4). Where did his joy come from? From their “partnership in furtherance of the Good News,” and from his confidence “that he who began a good work in you will complete it” (Philippians 1:5-6).

This kind of joy is contagious. When you think of the brothers and sisters in your small group, do you think of their problems first, or do you first thank God for them? One small group leader shared that leading her group used to exhaust her, because every week she was thinking about who hadn’t come and who wasn’t cooperating. Then she began to imitate Paul: before each prayer time, she named one thing she was thankful for in each member. Gradually she found that her attitude toward leading the group had changed—and the members became bolder about sharing.

There is a scene in the Old Testament book of Nehemiah: when the people heard the words of the Law, they all wept. But Nehemiah said, “Don’t be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10). He also told them to send portions of their feast to those who had nothing prepared. True joy is never kept to oneself; it flows out to others.

This week we have learned that joy rests on the Lord, that joy shares in heaven’s gladness, and that joy requires selflessness. Today, let this joy multiply: speak your thanks out loud, and let one brother or sister know that you thank God for them.
lessons.light: The final step in changing a mindset is multiplication. Joy that stays only in the heart slowly cools; when it is spoken and shared, it becomes strength for others. Giving thanks in everything lets God receive all the glory, and a simple “I thank God for you” is one of the warmest bricks we can lay as we build God’s system.
think: In Philippians 1:3-11, how is Paul’s joy connected to the way he sees the church?
When I think of the members of my church, does gratitude or criticism come to mind first?
To which two brothers or sisters will I say this week, “I thank God for you”?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for giving me brothers and sisters in Your house. Make me like Paul, thanking You every time I remember them and praying for them with joy. Let the joy that comes from You be my strength, and the strength of our church. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the name of every member of your small group or ministry team, and beside each one write something you thank God for. Then pick two of them and send a message: “I thanked God for you today, because…”
lessons.quick: The joy of the Lord is our strength.
text: I thank my God whenever I remember you,
always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy,
for your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now;
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.

It is even right for me to think this way on behalf of all of you, because I have you in my heart, because both in my bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the Good News, you all are partakers with me of grace.
For God is my witness, how I long after all of you in the tender mercies of Christ Jesus.
This I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment,
so that you may approve the things that are excellent, that you may be sincere and without offense to the day of Christ,
being filled with the fruits of righteousness which are through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

weeks.title: Peace: Pursuing Peace Wholeheartedly
weeks.keyText: So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.
weeks.theme: Peace is not the absence of disagreement, but choosing in Christ to build one another up rather than to beat one another.
group: Read Romans 14:13-19. How does Paul handle the Roman church’s disagreements over minor matters?
Think of a disagreement at church in which you chose silence, argument, or the pursuit of peace. What happened?
This week, how can we cross a “wall” in our small group or ministry team to build up one brother or sister?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, before entering the sanctuary, ask the Lord to let the peace of Christ rule in your heart. If there is tension between you and a fellow member, pray for them during the service. Afterward, greet a brother or sister from a different generation, a different background, or a different point of view, and speak one word that builds them up.

lessons.title: Pursue Peace, Build One Another Up
lessons.hear:
The church in Rome had a problem that seemed small but stirred up fierce arguments: what to eat and which days to observe. Some felt free to eat anything; others insisted on eating only vegetables. Some regarded certain days as special; others considered every day alike. Both sides believed they were doing it for the Lord, and the result was judging and despising one another.

Today’s church has its own “food issues”: traditional hymns or contemporary songs, in-person or online meetings, formal or casual dress on Sunday, which language to use from the pulpit, how to run the children’s Sunday school. Most of these are not foundational to salvation, yet they often wound the relationships between brothers and sisters.

Paul doesn’t rush to rule on who is right and who is wrong. Instead, he lifts our eyes higher: “for God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17). Then he concludes: “So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up” (Romans 14:19).

Notice the phrase “follow after.” Peace doesn’t just happen; we have to pursue it actively. Biblical peace is not merely the absence of quarreling; it is wholeness in relationships and mutual building up. A church might never argue and yet be cold and fragmented, everyone doing their own thing—that is not peace. Another church might hold differing opinions yet respect one another in love and grow together—that is the peace the Holy Spirit produces.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine His light on you: among the things I insist on, which are foundational to God’s Kingdom, and which are only my “eating and drinking”?
lessons.light: The self-centered treat their own tastes as truth, dressing up “preferences” as “principles”; the selfless discern what belongs to God’s Kingdom and what is merely eating and drinking. To let Jesus reign is to let His will rank above my habits. The key to peace is not who wins, but whether Christ is lifted up and the body is built up.
think: In Romans 14:13-19, what does Paul warn us not to do, and what does he urge us to pursue?
Which of the things I insist on at church are really just personal preferences?
How can I choose, in one small matter today, to build others up rather than insist on my own way?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are the Prince of Peace. Forgive me for so often valuing my own preferences above my brothers and sisters, judging and hurting others over small things. Help me discern what is foundational to Your Kingdom, gladly yield in everything else, pursue peace, and build up Your body. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down one issue where you often disagree with others at church. Ask yourself honestly: is this foundational to God’s Kingdom, or is it my preference? If it is a preference, surrender it to the Lord, and pray for the brother or sister who sees it differently.
lessons.quick: God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking; I will pursue peace and build others up.
text: Therefore let’s not judge one another any more, but judge this rather, that no man put a stumbling block in his brother’s way, or an occasion for falling.
I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean of itself; except that to him who considers anything to be unclean, to him it is unclean.
Yet if because of food your brother is grieved, you walk no longer in love. Don’t destroy with your food him for whom Christ died.
Then don’t let your good be slandered,
for God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable to God and approved by men.
So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.

lessons.title: The Wisdom from Above
lessons.hear:
A church decided to add a new worship band to its Sunday service. The young people were thrilled; the older members found it too loud and couldn’t make out the lyrics. Before long, each side was rallying support in its own group chats. Some said, “The young people don’t respect tradition.” Others said, “The older generation is blocking the church’s future.” At ministry team meetings everyone was politely civil, but afterward the conversations carried on in the parking lot.

When it comes to peace, we often hold one of two old mindsets. One is “silence means peace”: everyone bites their tongue, avoids the issue, and keeps up a surface calm. The other is “peace means I win”: once the other side accepts my view, the problem is solved. The first is a cold war; the second is conquest. Neither is biblical peace.

James identifies the root of the problem: “For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed” (James 3:16). Then he says, “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy” (James 3:17). True peace is first pure—our motives must be clean, with no factions and no manipulation; only then come gentleness, a willingness to listen, and freedom from partiality.

That church eventually invited representatives of both generations to pray together—before discussing any plans. The young worship band went to the seniors’ fellowship to learn a few old hymns, and the seniors agreed to lay hands on the worship team and bless them once a month. The song list was adjusted, but the bigger change was in their hearts: two generations began to pray for one another.

Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Peace is not avoiding conflict; it is walking into conflict with the wisdom from above.
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Keeping up a surface calm is self-centered self-protection; forcing the other side to give in is self-centered conquest. Selfless peace first purifies its own motives and then moves gently toward the other person. Every generation in the church is a “2” to the others.
think: What two kinds of wisdom does James 3:13-18 contrast, and what fruit does each produce?
When conflict arises at church, do I lean toward a cold war, or toward wanting to win?
How can I first “purify” my own motives before facing a disagreement?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, give me the wisdom that comes from above. Forgive me for wanting only to protect myself or to win in conflict, and even for joining factions and talking behind others’ backs. Purify my motives; make me gentle, reasonable, and without partiality—a peacemaker. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you are caught up in a disagreement at church, stop talking about it behind people’s backs, starting today. Spend five minutes praying for one brother or sister on “the other side,” asking God to bless them and to purify your motives.
lessons.quick: The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceful.
text: Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom.
But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth.
This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic.
For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

lessons.title: Becoming a Peacemaker
lessons.hear:
Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18). These words are gentle and very practical. “If it is possible” acknowledges that peace takes two: sometimes the other person is unwilling, and sometimes the hurt runs so deep that it needs time and the help of a third party. But “as much as it is up to you” reminds me to leave no room for excuses on my side.

In church life, peacemaking often begins with three small things:
1. Don’t be a messenger. When someone complains to you about another co-worker, don’t add fuel to the fire and don’t pass it on. Gently ask, “Would you be willing to talk with them directly? I’ll pray with you.”
2. Speak gently. Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). In a ministry team meeting, the same opinion lands completely differently when it begins with “I’m concerned that…” rather than “You always…”
3. Take the first step. Paul says, “Repay no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17), and “Be of the same mind one toward another” (Romans 12:16). Rather than waiting for the other person to apologize first, offer a greeting first.

One small group leader noticed that two members had stopped speaking to each other over the meeting time. Instead of mediating publicly in the group, he invited each of them out for coffee separately, listened fully to their hurts, and then invited the two of them to pray together. Afterward one of them said, “I don’t actually care that much about the time. I just felt like no one was listening to me.” Behind many conflicts is a heart that needs to be heard.

One caution: where spiritual abuse, harassment, or financial misconduct is involved, peacemaking does not mean the person who was harmed must stay silent. It means seeking a trustworthy third party or the church’s proper channels, so that truth and justice can come to light.
lessons.light: People matter more than tasks—never hurt people for the sake of a task. Peacemakers first find rest within themselves, and only then can they bring peace to others. This is the training of the “0” in 920: laying down our own grievances and pride and taking the first step toward the other person. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on the other person’s faults; when Jesus reigns in my heart, I don’t have to wait for others to change first.
think: In Romans 12:16-18, what do “if it is possible” and “as much as it is up to you” each remind me of?
Have I ever acted as a messenger at church and caused a conflict to grow?
Toward which brother or sister can I take the first step today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You broke down the dividing wall for us. Make me a peacemaker. Guard my mouth from carrying tales or adding fuel to the fire; give me gentle words and the courage to take the first step, and as much as it is up to me, help me be at peace with all people. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a greeting to a brother or sister with whom you have some tension or disagreement. Don’t bring up the issue—just say, “How have you been? I’m praying for you.” If someone complains to you about another person, encourage them to talk to that person directly.
lessons.quick: As much as it is up to me, I will be at peace with everyone.
text: Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.
Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.

lessons.title: When Paul and Barnabas Disagreed
lessons.hear:
The Bible is honest. It records the breakup of two great co-workers in the early church. Paul and Barnabas had risked their lives together and done mission together, yet over whether to take Mark along, “the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other” (Acts 15:39). Paul valued reliability for the mission; Barnabas valued restoring a person. Both had a point, but neither would give way.

This passage invites an honest review. In church conflicts, I often say I am “standing on principle.” How much of that is really about saving face, or about not wanting to give in? Do I hold on to people’s past failures—the way Paul remembered that Mark had once left them—and decide they can never be used again?

Abram in the Old Testament gives us another picture. His herdsmen and Lot’s herdsmen were quarreling. As the elder, Abram had every right to choose first, but he said, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.” (Genesis 13:8). Then he let Lot choose first. Yielding is not weakness; it is placing the relationship above our own interests and trusting God as our provider.

The story of Paul and Barnabas doesn’t end with the split. Years later, writing from prison to Timothy, Paul said, “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). Mark, once rejected, became Paul’s helper. This is the grace of reconciliation: God can heal rifts between co-workers and can restore honor to those who once failed.

The first step of adjustment is to admit that I had a part in it too. The second is to lay down “I have to be right” before the Lord. The third is to bless the person who parted ways with me and keep the door open.
lessons.light: Pride refuses to let go of “I’m right”; humility lays down power and returns to its proper place. Abram let God be God, and so he could yield. Paul’s later acceptance of Mark showed the maturing of a selfless life. Peace doesn’t always require that we serve together immediately, but it does require that I not shut the door to reconciliation.
think: How did Paul later view Mark? What change in Paul’s life does this reveal?
In which conflict did I dress up saving face as standing on principle?
How can I bless a co-worker who once parted ways with me?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, You see my stubbornness and resentment in conflict. Forgive me for so often assuming I am the one who is right, and for holding on to other people’s failures instead of letting them go. Give me Abram’s generous heart and the breadth Paul later showed, so that I bless those who once parted ways with me and keep the door to reconciliation open. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, think of a brother or sister with whom you had a conflict or parting of ways in ministry. Write down the part you played in it, confess it to the Lord, and pray one specific blessing over them.
lessons.quick: Yielding isn’t weakness; it puts the relationship above winning or losing.
text: After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

lessons.title: He Is Our Peace
lessons.hear:
The deepest wall in the early church was the one between Jews and Gentiles. Their food, customs, and histories clashed, and each looked down on the other. Yet Paul declares, “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation” (Ephesians 2:14). Peace in the church doesn’t rest on clever mediation skills; it is built on the cross.

Today’s church has many invisible walls too: between new members and longtime members, between congregations that worship in different languages, between older and younger believers, between professionals and blue-collar workers, even between those who attend in person and those who join online. Usually no one builds these walls on purpose. They form because we spend time only with people we know, and over time those circles harden into cliques.

The prophet Isaiah foretold the coming King long ago: “His name will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.” (Isaiah 9:6). The Prince of Peace doesn’t only bring peace to our hearts; He makes people who could never belong together into one within His body.

This week we have learned that peace is something we pursue, that it is wisdom from above, that it means doing all we can on our side, and that it means laying down “I have to be right.” Now pass on what you have received. The best way to multiply peace is to take someone across a wall with you: invite a brother or sister from a different background to share a meal, or tell your small group about an experience of reconciliation from this week. When people see Christians united across their differences, they see Jesus.
lessons.light: Building God’s system starts with tearing down walls. The self-centered build cliques; the selfless tear down walls. The “2” in 920 includes not only the people I know well, but also the people on the other side of the wall. When we are one in Christ, God’s will is done on earth as it is in heaven.
think: According to Ephesians 2:14-18, how did Christ make peace?
What invisible wall exists in my church life?
This week, which brother or sister “on the other side of the wall” will I invite, and to do what?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are our peace; on the cross You broke down the dividing wall. Tear down the cliques and prejudices in my heart as well, and make me willing to move toward people who are different from me. Let our church be a witness of peace, so that people recognize You through our unity. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a brother or sister from a different generation or background—or someone you seldom talk with—to share a meal or a cup of tea. Listen to the story of their faith, and close by praying for each other.
lessons.quick: Christ broke down the wall; I will no longer build cliques.
text: For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation,
having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace,
and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.
He came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near.
For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father.

weeks.title: Patience: Bearing with One Another in Love
weeks.keyText: with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
weeks.theme: Just as God has been patient with me for so long, I wait for and support imperfect brothers and sisters with patient love.
group: Read Colossians 3:12-15. How is a patient, persevering heart connected to our identity as people who are “holy and beloved”?
At church, what kind of person or situation is most likely to make you lose patience?
This week, which brother or sister is our small group willing to walk alongside with patience and love? How exactly will we do it?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, before entering the sanctuary, recall how patient God has been with you over the years. During the service, if something tries your patience—a long announcement, a noisy child, an off-key hymn—treat it as a chance to practice patience and pray for the person involved. Afterward, speak a gentle word to a brother or sister who often makes you impatient.

lessons.title: Putting On a Patient Heart
lessons.hear:
Paul wrote to the church in Ephesus, “with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2). Writing to the church in Colossae, he used almost the same list: “Put on therefore … a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance” (Colossians 3:12). Clearly, in the early church patience was not extra credit for the spiritually refined; it was a required course in church life.

Why does the church especially need patience? Because the church is made up of people who are still being changed. Small group leaders forget to reply to messages, pastors make mistakes in their sermons, the choir sings off-key, newcomers ask the same questions over and over, and veteran co-workers dig in their heels. Paul is very practical: “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any” (Colossians 3:13). He doesn’t pretend there will be no complaints in the church; he tells us what to do when there are.

Biblical patience isn’t gritting our teeth and bottling up anger. It means being “slow to anger” and willing to wait a long time. This is first of all God’s own character. On Mount Sinai God proclaimed to Moses, “The LORD! The LORD, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). Again and again Israel fell, and again and again God waited for them to return.

Notice that before Paul gives the command, he reminds us of our identity: “as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved” (Colossians 3:12). The power to be patient doesn’t come from my self-discipline; it flows from the fact that God has been patient with me for a long time. Someone who often remembers how much God has borne with them is far less likely to lose patience with their brothers and sisters.
lessons.light: In the “9” of 920, patience follows right after love, joy, and peace. The self-centered measure everything by their own timetable and grow impatient when others are slow; the selfless know they too are living under God’s patient waiting. To let Jesus reign is to let Him—not me—set the pace at which others change.
think: In Colossians 3:12-15, what identity does Paul remind us of before he calls us to patience?
In which areas of my life has God been patient with me for a long time?
Toward which brother or sister will I deliberately be “slow to anger” today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, You are slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness. Thank You for being patient with me and waiting for me all these years. Help me remember that I am beloved, and treat the brothers and sisters who try my patience the way You have treated me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three ways God has been patient with you over a long time. Then write the name of a brother or sister you have recently lost patience with, and pray over the two lists together.
lessons.quick: God has been patient with me for so long—so I can be patient with others.
text: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.
And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

lessons.title: Patient Toward All
lessons.hear:
In one small group there was a brother whose sharing always circled back to the same complaints: work wasn’t going well, his family didn’t understand him, no one at church cared about him. After six months of this, the other members began exchanging glances whenever he opened his mouth. One of them said privately, “I’ve been patient for a long time. Surely patience has its limits.”

We often hold two old mindsets about patience. One is “patience means holding it in”: say nothing on the outside, keep a tally on the inside, and one day explode. The other is “patience means letting things slide”: never deal with anything, no matter what the other person does, until the problem grows bigger and bigger. Neither is biblical patience.

Paul says, “admonish the disorderly, encourage the faint-hearted, support the weak, be patient toward all” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). Notice that patience is placed right alongside admonishing, encouraging, and supporting. Patience is not doing nothing; it is choosing, within a long-suffering love, the response that fits what the other person needs. The unruly need admonishing, the discouraged need encouragement, the weak need support—and every one of them needs time.

This is exactly how God treats us. The psalmist says, “For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). It isn’t that God is unaware of our problems; He knows our weakness, and so He is willing to lead us slowly.

Eventually the leader of that small group took the brother out for a meal, just the two of them, and learned that his father had recently been diagnosed with a serious illness. He didn’t know how to ask for help, so he kept complaining. The leader didn’t rush to give advice; he simply said, “We’ll walk with you.” A few months later, that brother had become the most caring person in the group. Patience is often waiting long enough to hear someone’s whole story.
lessons.light: Change your perspective and you change your mindset: from “Why is he still like this?” to “How does God see him?” Self-centered patience counts how long I have endured; selfless patience looks at what the other person needs. People matter more than tasks: the small group’s schedule can slow down, but no one should be given up on.
think: What kinds of people does 1 Thessalonians 5:14 mention, and what response does each need?
Is my patience more like “holding it in” or “letting things slide”?
What part of the story of the person who tries my patience might I not have heard yet?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You know how I am made, and still You are patient with me. Forgive me for so often keeping a tally in my heart, losing patience with my brothers and sisters, and even giving up on them. Give me wisdom to discern and a love that lasts, so that I am willing to hear someone’s whole story and walk with them slowly. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose a brother or sister who tries your patience and invite them for a fifteen-minute conversation. Just listen; don’t teach. Ask, “What has been hardest for you lately? How can I pray for you?”
lessons.quick: Patience is often waiting long enough to hear someone’s whole story.
text: We exhort you, brothers: Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all.
See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always follow after that which is good for one another and for all.

lessons.title: Waiting Like a Farmer
lessons.hear:
James uses a very down-to-earth picture: “Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain” (James 5:7). A farmer doesn’t plant seeds today and dig them up tomorrow to see whether they have sprouted. He knows that life has its own seasons. What he can do is plow, sow, water—and then wait.

Growth in church life works the same way. A newcomer has been attending for two years and still isn’t baptized. A young co-worker is full of zeal but often speaks too bluntly. An older member keeps saying, “That’s not how we used to do it.” A new small group leader is stumbling through the first months. We are easily tempted to pull on the sprouts to make them grow faster: pushing, correcting, or simply replacing people.

James goes on to say something crucial: “Don’t grumble, brothers, against one another, so that you won’t be judged” (James 5:9). Grumbling is impatience’s most common outlet—complaining in the group chat, making a snide remark at a ministry team meeting, venting to our family at home. Grumbling doesn’t make anyone grow faster; it only hardens the soil.

Today’s practice has three steps:
1. Take the long view: picture that brother or sister five years from now, and ask God how He intends to shape them.
2. Trade grumbling for intercession: every time you feel like complaining about them, pray one sentence for them instead.
3. Do one act of watering: offer a word of encouragement, some practical help, or simply your company.

One sister who walked with a newcomer for three years said that in the end she didn’t bring him to baptism by persuasion, but through three years of rides to church, birthday cards, and countless “That’s okay—see you next week.” The farmer’s patience finally received the early and late rain.
lessons.light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Patience trusts that the Holy Spirit’s work in others is more effective than my pushing. Relying on the Holy Spirit with the heart, we can wait; relying on ourselves with the head, we grow anxious. Handing the timetable to God is letting Jesus reign: my part is to water, and God’s part is to give the growth.
think: What examples does James 5:7-11 use to illustrate patience?
Toward which brother or sister have I recently felt the urge to force growth?
What one act of “watering” will I do for them today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, You are the God who makes life grow. Forgive me for so often being anxious and grumbling, wanting others to change at my pace. Make me like the farmer who plows, sows, and waters, and then waits in peace, entrusting the growth of every brother and sister into Your hands. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Choose a brother or sister you have grown a bit impatient waiting on. For the next seven days, each time you feel like grumbling about them, pray one sentence for them instead. Today, start by giving them one specific word of encouragement or one practical act of help.
lessons.quick: Grumbling hardens the soil; patience lets life grow.
text: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.
You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
Don’t grumble, brothers, against one another, so that you won’t be judged. Behold, the judge stands at the door.
Take, brothers, for an example of suffering and of perseverance, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.
Behold, we call them blessed who endured. You have heard of the perseverance of Job and have seen the Lord in the outcome, and how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

lessons.title: The Moment Moses Struck the Rock
lessons.hear:
The Bible describes Moses as “very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3). He led a constantly complaining people through the wilderness for nearly forty years. But at Kadesh, when the people quarreled yet again over the lack of water, he said to the assembly, “Hear now, you rebels! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” (Numbers 20:10). Then he raised his rod and struck the rock twice.

God had told him only to speak to the rock. Water still came out—God still had compassion on the people—but Moses’ anger kept him from honoring God as holy before them. Years of pent-up weariness and hurt erupted in that moment.

This is a mirror for those who have served a long time. The people most likely to lose patience are often not new believers but those who have served the longest and given the most. Moses’ words rise in our hearts too: “After all I’ve done for you…” Today, review honestly: Are my words growing sharper? Am I often sarcastic in the group chat? Have I let ministry fatigue turn into anger at my brothers and sisters? When I say “we,” have I quietly put myself in God’s place?

The path of adjustment starts with admitting that patience is not something I can hold together by willpower; it comes by grace. It also means facing my limits honestly, learning to share the load and to rest, so that weariness doesn’t build up into anger.

Moses’ story also has an ending full of grace. On Mount Nebo, God told him, “I have caused you to see it with your eyes” (Deuteronomy 34:4), showing him the Promised Land. And in the New Testament, Moses appears in glory on the Mount of Transfiguration, speaking with the Lord Jesus about the salvation He was about to accomplish (see Luke 9:30-31). God’s patience is longer than our failures.
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping God’s power. When Moses said, “Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” he put himself in God’s place in that moment. A lapse of patience is often the self-centered life piling up: my sacrifices, my grievances. When I return to my proper place and let God be God, I can serve people gently once again.
think: What do Moses’ words in Numbers 20:10 reveal about the state of his heart?
In which area of my service has weariness begun to turn into anger?
Where do I need to share the load or rest, and whom do I need to ask for help?
lessons.speak: Lord, You see the weariness and hurt in my service, and the moments when I have lost patience with my brothers and sisters. Forgive me for putting myself in Your place. Renew my strength, teach me to share the load and to rest, and let me be patient by Your grace rather than by my own effort. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, recall a moment this week when you lost your patience, and write down what you were really feeling. If you hurt someone, apologize to them tomorrow. If your weariness is heavy, reach out to your pastor or small group leader to talk about sharing the load.
lessons.quick: God’s patience is longer than my failures.
text: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

“Take the rod, and assemble the congregation, you, and Aaron your brother, and speak to the rock before their eyes, that it pour out its water. You shall bring water to them out of the rock; so you shall give the congregation and their livestock drink.”
Moses took the rod from before the LORD, as he commanded him.
Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly together before the rock, and he said to them, “Hear now, you rebels! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?”
Moses lifted up his hand, and struck the rock with his rod twice, and water came out abundantly. The congregation and their livestock drank.

The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Because you didn’t believe in me, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land which I have given them.”

lessons.title: Patience Displayed in Me
lessons.hear:
Looking back over his life in his later years, Paul said something astonishing: “However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). Saul, who had once persecuted the church, became a showcase of God’s patience.

These words turn our view of patience upside down. We usually think of patience as something we give to others; but Paul says that he himself was, first of all, someone who had been shown patience. God did not give up on him while he was persecuting the church, and the Lord did not replace Peter after he denied Him three times. Behind every one of us who now stands and serves in the church lies a long history of God’s waiting.

The apostle Peter also says, “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.” (2 Peter 3:9). God’s patience exists to give people a chance. When I am patient with a brother or sister at church, I am actually joining God in giving them a chance.

Over these past weeks we have looked at the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, and patience. These are not four separate lessons, but the same life of Christ taking shape in different situations. Today’s multiplication is simple: tell someone the story of how God has been patient with you. Perhaps it is a sister still waiting for her family to come to faith, or a small group leader about to give up on a member. Your testimony may be exactly what gives them strength to keep on being patient.
lessons.light: The complete picture of 920 is this: in every relationship with a “2,” practice the selfless “0,” and bear the “9”—the life of Christ. Patience gives this process time to happen. The final step in changing a mindset is multiplication: your story of being borne with by God becomes an example for those who come after.
think: According to Paul, for what purpose did Jesus display His patience in him?
Looking back on this week, how has my view of patience changed?
To whom—someone who needs it right now—will I tell the story of God’s patience with me?
