lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank You for displaying all Your patience in me. I too have obtained mercy. Let this grace take root in my heart, make me willing to join You in giving others a chance, and help me pass on the testimony of Your patience to brothers and sisters who are waiting or about to give up. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down an experience of God’s long patience with you in three to five sentences. Share it with your spiritual companion or with a brother or sister who is serving through a hard season, and pray for them.
lessons.quick: I have been shown patience, and I want to show patience to others.
text: I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he counted me faithful, appointing me to service,
although I used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. However, I obtained mercy because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.

weeks.title: Kindness: Be Kind to One Another
weeks.keyText: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.
weeks.theme: Kindness isn’t being good to those who deserve it, but taking the initiative, as God does, to show grace to the undeserving.
group: Read Ephesians 4:29-32. Why is kindness placed alongside “forgiving each other”?
In church, what kind of person is hardest for you to be kind to, and why?
Which forgotten member can our small group show kindness to together this week? Decide on one action.
weeks.sunday: Before Sunday, quietly recall how God forgave you in Christ. During the service, notice those sitting in the corner, the newcomers, and those who haven’t been around for a while. After the service, don’t rush to find your friends; walk over to one of them first and ask, “Could I have lunch with you today?” Bring the kindness of the King’s table into the Lord’s Day.

lessons.title: Be Kind to One Another
lessons.hear:
When Paul writes in Ephesians about putting off the old self and putting on the new, he doesn’t stay in the realm of abstract doctrine. He walks it straight into the most ordinary corners of church life: what comes out of our mouths, what we nurse in our hearts, how we treat one another. First he lists what has to go: “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). Notice the words “from you.” He isn’t talking about the world out there. He means the table at the ministry team meeting, the living room where the small group gathers, the chat window of the church group.

Then Paul describes the life that takes their place: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). The word “kind” carries the sense of something useful, beneficial, something that makes life easier for others. Kindness isn’t polite words. It is goodness that actually does the other person good. It is a warmth that takes the initiative and doesn’t wait for the other person to improve first.

The most important part of this verse is its foundation: “just as God also in Christ forgave you.” Kindness isn’t a naturally pleasant temperament. It flows out of the experience of being forgiven. Jesus once told a parable about a servant whose master canceled a debt of ten thousand talents—and who then walked out and grabbed a fellow servant by the throat over a hundred denarii (see Matthew 18:23-35). Someone who truly remembers how much he has been forgiven will find it very hard to keep clutching a brother’s hundred denarii.

Tucked in the middle is one more warning: “Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30). The cutting words and cold looks we trade with one another actually grieve the Spirit. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine His light on you: in your church, who is the hardest person for you to be kind to? You don’t need to rush to change him. First go back to the cross and receive afresh how kindly God has treated you.
lessons.light: In the “9” of 920, kindness is the fruit that makes life a little easier for others. The self-centered person asks, “Does he deserve it?” The selfless person asks, “How has God treated me?” Kindness doesn’t come from my good intentions; it is Christ living in me, showing grace through me to the “2”—the people around me. Only the forgiven can truly forgive.
think: In Ephesians 4:31-32, what are we told to put away, and what are we told to put on?
Who in my church is the hardest person for me to be kind to, and what reason does my heart give?
Remembering how God forgave me in Christ, what small step can I take toward that person today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for forgiving every debt I owed You in Christ. I confess that I am still holding on to bitterness and resentment, and toward some brothers and sisters I am merely polite, not kind. Holy Spirit, remove the malice in me. Help me remember how kindly You have treated me, so that I treat the brothers and sisters around me the same way. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the name of the person in your church you find hardest to be kind to. Under the name write: “God forgave me in Christ, and He forgave this person too.” Then spend one minute praying a blessing over that person, without mentioning any of their faults.
lessons.quick: Kindness flows from being forgiven; remember the cross and you can treat others well.
text: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.title: Kind to the Unthankful
lessons.hear:
A woman who had sung in the church choir for years once overheard another choir member say behind her back after rehearsal that she “loved the spotlight.” From that day on she was perfectly courteous to that member. But whenever the other woman was sick and missed practice, needing someone to mark her part or help her catch up on a phrase, she pretended not to notice. She told herself, “I’m not hurting her. I just don’t want to be nice to her.”

That is an old mindset we all know well: kindness is for the right people. If you’re good to me, I’ll be twice as good to you. If you’re not, I’ll keep my distance and not retaliate—and that already feels quite spiritual. But Jesus tears down that line with one sentence: “If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same” (Luke 6:33). Returning favor for favor isn’t kindness. It’s just an exchange.

God’s perspective turns everything upside down: “But love your enemies, and do good … for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil” (Luke 6:35). The clearest mark of God’s kindness is that it lands on people who don’t deserve it. We ourselves are the unthankful—how often we receive grace and forget it the moment we turn around, and still He is kind to us every day. Of course, kindness doesn’t mean letting people hurt you or pretending nothing happened. When harm is ongoing, we still need to set boundaries and seek help. But within those boundaries we can still choose to bless rather than to freeze someone out.

Later, during her Bible reading, this passage took hold of that choir member. The next time the other woman missed rehearsal, she sent a message on her own: “I’ve marked your part for you. When you’re back, I’ll practice it with you.” After a long pause came the reply: “I’m sorry.” Kindness didn’t demand an apology first, yet kindness often brings one out. Jesus closes with these words: “Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful” (Luke 6:36). Kindness is where children look most like their Father.
lessons.light: Self-centered kindness is a ledger: you were this good to me, so I’ll repay you that much. Selfless kindness is a spring: it doesn’t ask whether the other person deserves it; it looks only at the Father’s heart. Coldness breeds coldness, but kindness sets kindness in motion. To let Jesus reign is to let Him decide how I treat the person who has hurt me.
think: In Luke 6:32-36, which things does Jesus say “even sinners” do?
Toward which brothers or sisters have I merely “not retaliated,” without ever being kind?
What practical good thing can I do this week for someone who once made me uncomfortable?
lessons.speak: Merciful Father, You are kind to the unthankful—and that includes me. I confess that my goodness often keeps score, and toward those who have hurt me I have only coldness left. Give me the heart of Your child, to be merciful as You are merciful, and within healthy boundaries to reach out first without waiting for the other person to change. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of someone who once wronged you but is still in the same small group or ministry as you. Today, do one concrete small thing for them—pick up a drink for them, help organize their materials, pass along a helpful resource—without any explanation attached.
lessons.quick: Kindness isn’t an exchange; it’s treating the undeserving the way the Father does.
text: “If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.
If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same.
If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to receive back as much.
But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back; and your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil.
“Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful.

lessons.title: For Jonathan’s Sake
lessons.hear:
Once David was secure on his throne, he asked a highly unusual question: “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” (2 Samuel 9:3). In the ancient world, a new king would often wipe out the descendants of the previous dynasty to remove any future threat. David instead went looking for them, because he remembered the covenant he had made with Jonathan.

The one they found was Mephibosheth—lame in both feet, living far away in Lo Debar, long forgotten by everyone. He came before the king, fell on his face, and called himself a “dead dog” (2 Samuel 9:8). David answered, “Don’t be afraid; for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake … You will eat bread at my table continually” (2 Samuel 9:7). David didn’t hand him a sum of money and send him away. He gave him a seat at the king’s table.

This is exactly how God treats us in Christ. We are all the lame Mephibosheth, invited to the King’s banquet for the sake of Another. Practicing kindness means extending that table outward. Every church has its own Lo Debar: the elderly who haven’t been able to attend for years because of illness; the former ministry team member who quietly faded away after one conflict; the family no one has contacted since they moved; the person in the online gathering who never turns on their camera, whose name has been on the screen for months but whom no one has ever addressed.

Today’s assignment is to ask David’s question—“Is there yet any who is left?”—and then go looking. Don’t wait for that person to come back first, or to apologize first, or for the church to draw up a visitation schedule. You can make a phone call, set up a meal, or call them by name during the gathering. Sometimes a simple “We miss you” is an invitation back to the King’s table.
lessons.light: David showed kindness for Jonathan’s sake; we show kindness for Jesus’ sake. This is the selfless “0”: the motive isn’t whether I like this person, but that the Lord loves them. 920 begins with the forgotten “2” right around us. People matter more than tasks; one person brought back is more precious than a successful event.
think: In 2 Samuel 9, what did David take the initiative to do, and how did Mephibosheth respond?
Who are the forgotten people living in the Lo Debar of our church or small group?
Whom will I contact today, and how will I invite them back to the table?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I was once the lame Mephibosheth, invited to the Father’s table for Your sake. Open my eyes to see the forgotten people in my church, and give me courage to go looking for them—not out of duty, but out of Your lovingkindness. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact someone who hasn’t appeared in your gatherings or group chat for a long time. Call or send a private message: “We miss you. Could I take you out for a meal this week?” and set a specific time.
lessons.quick: Ask David’s question—“Is there yet any who is left?”—and then go find them.
text: David said, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
There was of Saul’s house a servant whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David; and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He said, “I am your servant.”
The king said, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan still has a son, who is lame in his feet.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar.”
Then King David sent and brought him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo Debar.
Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, fell on his face, and showed respect. David said, “Mephibosheth?” He answered, “Behold, your servant!”

David said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”

lessons.title: The Older Son Outside the Door
lessons.hear:
When we read the parable of the prodigal son, we usually focus on the younger son. But Jesus told it to a group of Pharisees who were grumbling that He welcomed sinners and ate with them (see Luke 15:1-2). So the story’s real ending rests on a man standing outside the door, angry: “But he was angry, and would not go in. Therefore his father came out, and begged him” (Luke 15:28).

The older son never left home and never squandered anything; by the rules, he was beyond reproach. All he lacked was kindness. He said, “These many years I have served you,” and then “this your son”—he couldn’t even bring himself to say “my brother.” How much this resembles certain moments in church. A veteran ministry team member watches a young newcomer quickly given major responsibility and mutters, “We had to wait years for that.” A longtime member sees someone who once left come back, and while everyone rejoices, he says coldly, “Back now that he’s had his fun.” Different generations can’t stand each other’s clothes, songs, or ways of talking.

This is where the review begins. Am I living in the Father’s house without having the Father’s heart? Have my years of service quietly turned into a ledger in my heart? When someone else receives grace, is my first reaction joy or resentment?

The way to adjust is found in the father’s reply: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found” (Luke 15:31-32). The father didn’t scold him. He came out personally and pleaded with him, treating his unkind son with kindness. Paul says that the kindness of God leads us to repentance (see Romans 2:4). Today, let that kindness lead you through the door to sit at the feast with the brother who has come home.
lessons.light: The older son’s problem was the self-centered life: he put his own effort at the center and felt his father owed him. That kind of pride often wears the costume of “faithful service.” The selfless know: I serve because I have received grace, not to earn status. When we return to our proper place as sons and daughters, we can rejoice for our brother; when our relationship with God is right, our relationships with others can be made right.
think: In Luke 15:25-32, how does the older son refer to his brother, and how does the father refer to him?
When newcomers, young people, or those who return receive grace, do I feel resentment?
How can I express welcome to someone who is new or has come back?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that I am often like the older son. I have served in Your house for years, yet my heart has been keeping accounts, and I can’t bear to see others receive grace. Thank You for not scolding me, but coming out to plead with me. Take away my comparing and resentment, and give me Your heart to rejoice over everyone who comes home. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, find someone in your church or small group who is new, young, or has recently returned. Say a specific word of welcome or encouragement to them in person, and ask, “Is there anything I can help you with?”
lessons.quick: Living in the Father’s house without the Father’s heart—this is where I need to repent.
text: “Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing.
He called one of the servants to him and asked what was going on.
He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’
But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and begged him.
But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.
But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’
“He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’”

lessons.title: When Kindness Appeared
lessons.hear:
Paul wrote to Titus, who was pastoring on Crete, where the churches were not easy to lead. He reminded Titus—and everyone who has been rubbed the wrong way by people in church, and has rubbed others the wrong way too: “For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived … living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another” (Titus 3:3). That was our past, and it is often what we carelessly slide back into.

The turning point comes in the next sentence: “But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared, not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us” (Titus 3:4-5). Kindness is not merely a virtue. It has a name and a face—Jesus Christ. When God’s kindness “appeared,” it means He Himself came and walked among us.

This week we have seen several faces of kindness. It flows from being forgiven (see Ephesians 4:32). It is kind to the unthankful (see Luke 6:35). It goes looking for the forgotten Mephibosheth. And it gently pleads with the resentful older son to come inside. In the end, kindness means letting others see God’s kindness “appear” once again in me. Paul says, “Love is patient and is kind” (1 Corinthians 13:4). Patience doesn’t strike back; kindness reaches out.

Multiplication means letting kindness become the culture of the church, not just the good deeds of individuals. You can share what you have received this week with your small group, or invite a companion to join you in doing one thing every week for a “forgotten person.” When one person learns kindness, a small group gains warmth. When a small group learns kindness, the whole church becomes a place people want to come home to.
lessons.light: The last of the eight steps of changing a mindset is multiplication. If kindness stays as a feeling in the heart, it hasn’t yet borne fruit. The “9” of 920 must be tasted by the “2”—let the people connected to you taste God’s kindness in your words, attitudes, and actions. In this way, all the glory goes to the Lord who was kind to us first.
think: In Titus 3:3-7, on what basis did God save us, and on what basis did He not?
Which picture of kindness this week moved me most, and how have I changed?
Whom will I invite to join me in regularly showing kindness to a forgotten person?
lessons.speak: Jesus my Savior, You are God’s kindness made visible. I was once hateful and hating others, yet You saved me according to Your mercy. Let Your kindness be seen in me, and through me pass it on to my small group and the next generation, so that our church becomes a place people want to come home to. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, meet with your spiritual companion or a small group member and share what you received about kindness this week. Together choose one brother or sister who needs care, and agree on who will call, who will bring a meal, and who will spend time with them this week.
lessons.quick: Kindness has a face—Jesus; let others see Him in me.
text: For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared,
not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,
whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior;
that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

weeks.title: Goodness: Especially to the Household of Faith
weeks.keyText: So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.
weeks.theme: Goodness isn’t just being a nice person; it is putting love into action without giving up, beginning with God’s household.
group: Read Galatians 6:7-10. What do “not be weary” and “don’t give up” say to you?
Have you ever grown discouraged in doing good? What made you want to quit?
What practical thing can our small group do together this week for a brother or sister in need in the household of faith?
weeks.sunday: Before Sunday, ask the Lord to show you one concrete need in your church: not enough hands to stack chairs, a newcomer with no one to show them to a seat, an older member who can’t find a place to sit. During the service, pray quietly: “Lord, when it is in the power of my hand to do good, don’t let me hold back.” After the service, don’t first ask who is in charge—just do one thing.

lessons.title: Sowing to the Spirit
lessons.hear:
After describing the fruit of the Spirit, Paul closes with a farmer’s picture: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7). Church life is like a field. Some people sow complaints, comparison, and coldness week after week, and in time they harvest a weary, guarded community. Others quietly sow care, prayer, and practical help. It may not sprout right away, but in some season it grows into a grove of trees that gives shade.

Goodness is love turned into action. Love is the direction of the heart; goodness is the movement of the hand. The psalmist praises God this way: “You are good, and do good” (Psalm 119:68). God’s goodness doesn’t stay locked inside His attributes; it shows up in everything He does. So a person who has been changed by God’s goodness also begins to do good.

Then Paul says something every ministry team member can relate to: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9). Why would he need to say that? Because doing good is often exhausting, and often no one notices. A children’s ministry teacher spends a whole evening preparing a lesson, and the kids are noisy the entire time. The brother running the sound desk gets no comment when everything goes right, but the whole room knows when something goes wrong. Discouragement is the most common temptation of those who do good.

Finally Paul sets the priority: “So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith” (Galatians 6:10). He isn’t telling us to care only for our own. He is saying that a church that won’t even be good to the brothers and sisters right beside it will find it very hard to convince the world that its goodness is real. Goodness starts in God’s household, and then flows outward.
lessons.light: “Sowing to the Spirit” means relying on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the head. When we do good in our own strength, we soon start keeping score and wearing out; when we do good by the Spirit, the strength wells up from within without end. Goodness is the “9” of 920 bearing fruit in our hands, so that the “2” around us receive real, practical help.
think: In Galatians 6:7-10, what words does Paul use that relate to sowing and reaping?
What kind of seeds have I mostly been sowing in my church lately?
In the household of faith, to whom can I sow a seed of goodness this week?
lessons.speak: Father, You are good, and Your goodness comes to me every day. I confess that I often grow discouraged in doing good, feeling that no one notices and it isn’t worth it. Holy Spirit, renew my strength. Help me sow to the Spirit, not growing weary or giving up, and to put love into action first in Your household. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray over one ministry you are serving in, or once laid down, at church: “Lord, give me a heart that doesn’t give up.” Then send a specific word of thanks to a ministry team member who serves faithfully and quietly in the same role.
lessons.quick: Goodness is love put into action; sow to the Spirit and don’t give up.
text: Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.
For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.

lessons.title: Love Without Hypocrisy
lessons.hear:
We often praise someone by saying, “He’s such a nice person”: even-tempered, never offends anyone, always smiling when you see him. But in the Bible, goodness goes far deeper than being nice. Paul gets straight to the point: “Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good” (Romans 12:9). Goodness isn’t politeness that avoids conflict. It is a life that clings to what is good and turns away from what is evil.

In one small group there was a brother everyone called Mr. Nice Guy. He never missed a meeting, and whenever it was his turn to share he said, “All good, praise the Lord.” One time, a young member had been out of work for three months and could barely pay rent. He hinted in the group chat, asking everyone to pray. Mr. Nice Guy replied with a praying-hands sticker, and that was it. In the end it was a sister who was usually blunt—often criticized for being “too much”—who called him privately to find out exactly what he needed. She gathered a few people to cover a month’s rent, then helped him rework his résumé and practice for interviews.

Which of them was the good person? The old mindset says goodness means not doing bad things and not offending anyone. God’s perspective says goodness means actually doing good. Paul goes on to describe what goodness looks like: “In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another” (Romans 12:10), and “contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.” (Romans 12:13). These are all action words, and every one of them costs time, money, or pride.

This doesn’t mean everyone has to become pushy. It means asking: is my “niceness” protecting my image, or is it actually doing my brother good? A sticker can express care, but if I have the means to help and stop at the sticker, love has become hypocritical. Proverbs says, “Don’t withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it” (Proverbs 3:27).
lessons.light: For a self-centered “nice person,” the center of niceness is the self: I don’t want the hassle, I don’t want to be rejected, I don’t want to pay the price. Selfless goodness puts the other person at the center: What does he need? What can I give? People matter more than tasks, and a brother’s real need matters more than my convenience and my image.
think: In Romans 12:9-13, which concrete actions require paying a price?
How much of my “niceness” is about protecting my own image?
What need around me do I have the means to meet, yet I have only been “praying about it”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You went about doing good, never merely talking about it. I confess that my love often stops at politeness and stickers, afraid of the hassle and the cost. Remove the hypocrisy from my love. Help me cling to what is good, and be willing to reach out my hands to meet the needs of my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Recall a need you recently saw in your small group or church group chat. Today, contact that person privately and ask specifically, “What can I do to help you?” and follow through on one thing this week.
lessons.quick: Goodness isn’t being nice; it’s actually doing good.
text: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,
not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,
rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer,
contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.

lessons.title: The Garments in Dorcas’s Hands
lessons.hear:
In Joppa there was a disciple named Dorcas. Luke introduces her in a single sentence: “This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did” (Acts 9:36). There is no record of her preaching, and she held no leadership title. Yet when she died, she drew the most genuine tears in the whole church.

When Peter arrived in the upper room, the scene was deeply moving: “All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.” (Acts 9:39). They didn’t bring out her achievements. They brought out piece after piece of clothing. Every stitch and every thread was a good deed Dorcas had done, in ordinary days, for those who had no one else to depend on.

Practicing goodness is often just this concrete and this ordinary. In one church, a retired auntie has made a pot of soup and delivered it every time a member gives birth, has surgery, or loses a loved one—without a break for more than twenty years. A young man who works at a tech company spends half an hour every week teaching older members how to join the online gatherings on their phones. These things never make it into the bulletin, but stitch by stitch they weave the garment of the church.

Today’s assignment is to do a “Dorcas-style” good deed: find a brother or sister with a practical need and serve them with what you have in your hands. If you can cook, bring a meal. If you know computers, go help an older member. If you have a car, give a ride to a sister who has trouble getting to church. Don’t wait until you have a large sum of money or a big plan before you do good. Jesus said that whatever we do for one of the least of His brothers, we do for Him (see Matthew 25:40).
lessons.light: In the Way of Service, “Life” means cultivating and living out the life of Jesus. Dorcas’s life let people see Jesus, so when her story spread, “many believed in the Lord” (Acts 9:42). Unnoticed goodness inside the church naturally becomes the most powerful witness to those outside, and the glory goes to God.
think: In Acts 9:36-42, how did the widows describe Dorcas’s life?
What skills, time, or resources do I have in my hands that I can use to do good?
Which brother or sister will I serve today with what I have?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank You for showing me the ordinary yet beautiful life of Dorcas. What I have in my hands isn’t much, but I offer it to You to use. Lead me today to serve a brother or sister in need, so that through my small act they may touch Your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose a brother or sister with a practical need (new parents, an older member who is ill, a family that just moved). Use your skills or resources to do one concrete thing for them, and complete it this week.
lessons.quick: Don’t wait for something big; use what’s in your hands to sew a garment of love.
text: Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated means Dorcas. This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did.
In those days, she became sick and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
As Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, imploring him not to delay in coming to them.

Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.
Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up.
He gave her his hand and raised her up. Calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
This became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.

lessons.title: Passed By on the Other Side
lessons.hear:
In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the people who sting the most aren’t the robbers but two religious men: “By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side” (Luke 10:31). The Levite who came next did the same. It wasn’t that they didn’t see him. They saw him—and chose to go around.

We don’t know their reasons, but we can guess. Perhaps they were hurrying to serve at the temple. Perhaps they feared touching blood and becoming unclean, which would keep them from their duties. Perhaps they thought, “This isn’t my responsibility; someone will take care of it.” These reasons sound reasonable, even spiritual. And this is exactly the trap church people fall into most easily: busy with ministry, we walk right around people. We can be so busy rehearsing songs that we don’t notice a choir member whose eyes have been red and swollen for weeks. We can be so busy discussing an event’s schedule at the team meeting that we forget to ask the person in charge, “How are things at home?”

Review honestly: is there someone lately whom I “saw, and passed by on the other side”? Someone posted in the group that a family member was in the hospital, and I scrolled past. On Sunday I saw a newcomer standing alone, and I thought, “That’s what the welcome team is for.” I knew a ministry team member was about to collapse, and I figured, “That’s the pastor’s job.”

The way to adjust is right there in the parable: “But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion” (Luke 10:33). Goodness begins with seeing, moves through compassion, and ends with coming near. Jesus closes with, “Go and do likewise” (Luke 10:37). The good news is that Jesus Himself is the Samaritan who stopped. When we repent, He doesn’t condemn us; He sends us back out on the road—and this time we don’t go around.
lessons.light: Going around people for the sake of tasks is a common form of the self-centered life in church: the ministry becomes my achievement, and people become my interruption. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. To let Jesus reign is to let Him interrupt my schedule and bring me to the side of the one lying by the road.
think: In Luke 10:30-37, what is the difference between the priest, the Levite, and the Samaritan?
Whom have I recently “seen but passed by”? What reason did I give myself?
How will I turn back today and come near to care for that person?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are the Samaritan who stopped to save me. I confess that I am often swept along by ministry and schedules, seeing a need but passing by on the other side. Forgive me, and give me a heart that is moved with compassion, willing to stop for people and no longer neglect people for the sake of tasks. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a brother or sister you “saw but didn’t respond to.” Reach out and say honestly, “I saw your message that day and didn’t respond. I’m sorry. How have you been?”
lessons.quick: Goodness begins with seeing and becomes real the moment we stop.
text: Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

lessons.title: Let Good Works Light the House
lessons.hear:
Jesus said, “Neither do you light a lamp, and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house” (Matthew 5:15). The lamp shines first on “all who are in the house.” Goodness works the same way: it shines first in God’s household, and then that household becomes “a city located on a hill” that people far away can see.

This week, from the picture of sowing, we saw that goodness is love put into action. From Romans we saw that goodness isn’t just being nice, but clinging to what is good and meeting real needs. From Dorcas we saw that ordinary hands can stitch an extraordinary witness. And from the two men who went around, we saw our own detours. The source of goodness has never been us; it is Jesus, who “went about doing good” (Acts 10:38).

Jesus says the purpose of this light is “that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). This is the heart of 321: let Jesus receive all the glory. If we do good to be seen and praised, the lamp is shining on ourselves. Only when our good works let people see the Father is the lamp truly set on its stand.

The way to multiply is to make goodness something we do together. Paul says, “But you, brothers, don’t be weary in doing what is right” (2 Thessalonians 3:13). Doing good alone wears us out quickly; doing good together lets us go the distance. This week you could invite your small group to take on one thing together: visit an older member who lives alone once a month, take turns bringing meals to new parents, or reach out together to the people in the online group who never say a word. You could also share this week’s passages with the teenagers or children you lead, so that the next generation learns to do good by watching you do it.
lessons.light: Changing a mindset has to go all the way to multiplication: from me doing good alone, to us doing good together, to the next generation learning to do good as well. The companionship of 235 means people who sow together and refuse to give up together. The lamp sits on the stand, and the glory goes to the Father in heaven, not to the one who lit it.
think: In Matthew 5:14-16, what is the purpose of the light?
What is the biggest new insight I received about goodness this week?
Whom will I invite to join me in doing one good work on a regular basis?
lessons.speak: Father in heaven, thank You for making me the light of the world. Let my good works light up Your household and shine on those outside the door, so that what people see is not me, but You. Give me companions on the journey, so that together we do good without growing weary, and let the next generation learn goodness from us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, invite a small group member or spiritual companion to take on an ongoing good work with you (such as visiting an older member once a month). Set the date for your first action and put it on your calendar.
lessons.quick: Light God’s house first, and the city on the hill will be seen.
text: “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

weeks.title: Faithfulness: Faithful in Small Things
weeks.keyText: Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
weeks.theme: Faithfulness isn’t about doing great things, but about being reliable in the small things the Lord entrusts to us—keeping our word and doing what we say.
group: Read 1 Corinthians 4:1-5. Who does Paul say is the one who judges a steward?
In church ministry, in what kind of “small things” am I most likely to be unreliable?
Which promise we’ve made can we remind each other about and complete together this week?
weeks.sunday: Before Sunday, think back over the things you promised your church or fellow members this week—did you forget any of them? During the service, give thanks for God’s faithfulness: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). If you have a serving role, arrive early; and after the service, if you made a promise, make it good or explain in person.

lessons.title: Required of Stewards
lessons.hear:
The Corinthian church was very good at comparing. Some said, “I follow Paul,” others, “I follow Apollos.” They critiqued preachers the way people critique performers on a stage: who speaks best, who is most gifted, who has the most charisma. But Paul turned everyone’s eyes back where they belonged: “So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants and stewards of God’s mysteries” (1 Corinthians 4:1).

A steward is not the owner. Everything in his hands has been entrusted to him: time, gifts, positions—and people. So the measure of a steward isn’t how talented he is, but this: “Here, moreover, it is required of stewards, that they be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). The Greek word for “faithful” shares its root with the fruit of the Spirit that Paul calls pistis—faith, or faithfulness (Galatians 5:22). Faithfulness means being someone the Master can entrust things to without worry.

This turns the church’s values about ministry completely upside down. God doesn’t first look at whether you serve on stage or behind the scenes, whether you lead a hundred people or three. He looks at whether you are reliable in the post He has entrusted to you. A brother who arrives early every week to turn on the air conditioning and set up the chairs, and a sister who has faithfully compiled the prayer list every month for ten years, are seen by God just as clearly as the one standing in the pulpit.

Paul goes on to say that he doesn’t care about being judged by people; he doesn’t even judge himself, “but he who judges me is the Lord” (1 Corinthians 4:4). Faithful people live under the Lord’s gaze. When they are praised, they don’t get carried away; when no one sees, they don’t stop. And the reason we can be faithful is that God has been faithful to us first: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). Our faithfulness is a response to His.
lessons.light: The proud want to be the owner; the faithful are glad to be stewards. When we return to our proper place as stewards, we won’t become proud or insecure over the size of our role; we’ll care only whether the Master can rely on us. To let Jesus reign is to acknowledge that everything has been entrusted by Him, and that I will give Him an account.
think: In 1 Corinthians 4:1-5, how does Paul view people’s opinions and the Lord’s judgment?
In church, do I care more about people’s opinions or about what the Lord has entrusted to me?
Among the responsibilities the Lord has given me, which one needs me to be more reliable?
lessons.speak: Faithful Father, Your mercies are new every morning, and You have never once failed me. I confess that I often care about what people think and grow careless in small things. Make me a faithful steward, reliable in the post You have entrusted to me—not to be seen by people, but for You alone. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list every responsibility you carry in your church, small group, or online group (no matter how small). Next to each, write “Entrusted by the Lord,” and for the one you most often neglect, set a specific plan to do better.
lessons.quick: The Lord doesn’t ask how outstanding I am, only how reliable I am.
text: So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants and stewards of God’s mysteries.
Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by a human court. Yes, I don’t even judge my own self.
For I know nothing against myself. Yet I am not justified by this, but he who judges me is the Lord.

Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts. Then each man will get his praise from God.

lessons.title: Faithful in Very Little
lessons.hear:
In the small group chat, the leader asked, “Who can bring snacks next week?” One brother quickly replied, “I’ll do it!” When the day came, there were no snacks, and no brother either—not even a word of explanation. The next time, the leader asked, “Who can lead worship?” and he was the first to raise his hand again. The leader ended up quietly asking a sister to “be ready, just in case.” Over time, no one entrusted him with anything important, and he felt the small group “never gave him a chance.”

Many of us carry an old mindset deep down: small things don’t matter; real ministry is the big, visible stuff. When I get the chance to preach, lead a small group, or join the ministry team, I’ll give it everything. But Jesus says, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much” (Luke 16:10). Small things aren’t a rehearsal for big things. Small things are the test itself.

Proverbs uses a vivid picture to describe the cost of unreliability: “Confidence in someone unfaithful in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a lame foot” (Proverbs 25:19). A loose tooth can’t bite, and a sprained foot can’t walk. A team member who doesn’t follow through will leave the whole team unable to hold up just when it matters most. Faithfulness isn’t only a personal virtue; it is a joint in the body. When a joint is unstable, the whole body hurts.

God’s perspective is that reliability is itself a form of love. When you show up on time, you honor other people’s time. When you let people know early that you can’t make it, you protect the way the team works together. When you reply to messages and follow up on prayer requests, you tell people, “You can count on me.” This doesn’t mean we must be flawless. It means being honest and dependable—and saying so when we can’t do something.
lessons.light: Wanting only to do big things and disdaining small ones is the pride of the self-centered life: what I want is to be seen, not to be entrusted. The selfless know that being faithful in small things is letting Jesus reign—great or small, it’s all done for Him. Relationships are built on trust, and trust is built one small thing at a time.
think: In Luke 16:10-12, what does Jesus call “a very little”?
Is there something I promised to do but neither did nor explained?
Which “small promise” must I keep this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You never break Your word; everything You say will surely come to pass. I confess that I often look down on small things and fail to do what I promised. Forgive me. Make me someone my brothers and sisters can depend on, who does what I say, and who is honest when I can’t. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find one thing you promised to do but haven’t done yet (replying to a message, bringing something, following up on a prayer request) and finish it right away. If it’s already too late, explain and apologize to the person.
lessons.quick: Small things aren’t a rehearsal for big things—they are the test.
text: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?
If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?

lessons.title: Let Your Yes Be Yes
lessons.hear:
In the parable of the talents, the servant who received five talents and the one who received two receive exactly the same praise: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matthew 25:21). The master isn’t looking at how much they gained, but at whether they were faithful. From eternity’s perspective, all our ministry is “a few things,” yet it is exactly where the Lord measures us.

The most basic practice of faithfulness is found in our mouths. Jesus said, “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). In church life, that includes at least three things. First, don’t say yes lightly—before you say “I’ll do it,” check your calendar, ask your family, and ask the Lord. Second, once you say yes, follow through—on time, completely, and with a report back. Third, if you can’t do it, say so early—don’t let the team discover at the last minute that no one is there.

The Old Testament describes the person who may dwell on God’s holy hill as one who “keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change” (Psalm 15:4). One brother promised to unlock the church early one Saturday morning a month to prepare the room for the prayer meeting. Later he changed jobs and often worked late on Friday nights, but he still set his alarm and never once left the people who came to pray standing outside. He said, “This is my covenant with the Lord, and with my brothers and sisters.”

Today’s practice is very concrete: examine all your “yeses.” Are there some you said too quickly and can’t actually keep? Honestly adjust them—hand them back or ask someone to share the load. That isn’t failure; that is faithfulness. Are there some you agreed to but keep putting off? Finish one today. Let your “yes” carry weight again.
lessons.light: Faithfulness is the fruit the “2” around you can feel most: people can hand you things without worry. Doing what you say isn’t a matter of gritting your teeth with willpower; it means relying on the Spirit with your heart—asking Him before you say yes, and doing it for the Lord as you carry it out. That kind of “yes” is a “yes” that lets Jesus reign.
think: In Matthew 25:19-23, what is the same in the master’s words of praise to the two servants?
Do I often say “sure” too quickly and then fail to follow through?
Which commitment will I complete, or honestly adjust, today?
lessons.speak: Lord, I want to be a good and faithful servant. Govern my mouth, so that my “yes” truly means yes and my “no” truly means no. Teach me to ask You before I say yes, to rely on You to finish what I’ve agreed to, and to have the courage to be honest when I can’t. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, look through your calendar and message history and list every commitment you’ve made to your church or to brothers and sisters. Finish one you’ve been putting off, and for one you can’t keep, explain honestly and ask someone to share it.
lessons.quick: Ask first, then say yes; once you say yes, follow through.
text: “Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them.
He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’
“He also who got the two talents came and said, ‘Lord, you delivered to me two talents. Behold, I have gained another two talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things. I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’

lessons.title: Mark, Who Left Halfway
lessons.hear:
As a young man, Mark went out on mission with Paul and Barnabas, but he left them partway through, in Pamphylia, and went back to Jerusalem (see Acts 13:13). Later, when Barnabas wanted to take him along again, Paul refused: “But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work” (Acts 15:38). The two spiritual leaders even parted ways over it. One broken commitment cost a young man dearly.

Reading this, many of us see ourselves in Mark. We once agreed to serve and then dropped out halfway. We once took on a responsibility at a team meeting and disappeared as soon as the pressure came. We once quietly stopped answering messages just when the small group leader needed us most. Maybe there is a voice inside you that keeps saying, “I’m an unreliable person. God won’t use me again.”

But the story doesn’t end there. Barnabas didn’t give up on Mark; he took him along and kept going. Years later, Paul wrote to Timothy from prison: “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). The one who had once left halfway became a co-worker Paul could rely on in his final years.

The purpose of review isn’t self-condemnation; it is to return to the Lord’s faithfulness: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). The way to adjust has three steps: admit your unfaithfulness without making excuses; if it affected the team, go personally to explain and apologize; and start again with one small thing, rebuilding trust little by little. And if you are the team member someone once let down, ask the Lord for Barnabas’s eyes. Forgiveness doesn’t mean immediately handing the heavy load back, but it can give someone a path to being trusted again.
lessons.light: The greatest temptation after breaking faith is to hide—behind pride or behind insecurity: “That’s just the way I am.” The selfless don’t hide. They first come before God and confess, then go back to people and make repairs. God’s faithfulness isn’t an excuse for our unfaithfulness; it is the ground on which we stand up again.
think: From Acts 15 to 2 Timothy 4, how did Mark’s life change?
Is there a time I broke my word that I still haven’t faced or repaired?
With what small thing can I start rebuilding others’ trust in me?
lessons.speak: Faithful Lord, even when we are faithless, You remain faithful. I bring to You the ministries I abandoned halfway and the promises I broke, and I ask for Your forgiveness. Give me courage to make repairs, and give me Barnabas’s heart, willing to offer those who once let me down a way back. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a time you broke your word and haven’t made it right. Today, contact the ministry team member or brother or sister involved, briefly acknowledge it and apologize, then ask, “Is there anything I can do now to make up for it?”
lessons.quick: Even when I am faithless, the Lord stays faithful; start again with one small thing.
text: After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.

lessons.title: Entrust to Faithful People
lessons.hear:
Paul’s final charge to Timothy before his death was a chain passed down through four generations: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others. Whether this chain keeps going depends on one word: faithful. Paul then uses the pictures of a soldier, an athlete, and a hardworking farmer—all three of whom need day-after-day perseverance.

This week we have seen several sides of faithfulness. It is the steward’s duty, lived under the Lord’s gaze. It is tested in the smallest things. It begins with our “yes” and our “no.” And even when we have failed, God’s faithfulness still gives us a way to start again. Now faithfulness needs to be passed on through me.

What spiritual legacy needs most is not necessarily the most gifted people, but the most reliable ones. A sister who has led children’s ministry for more than ten years says her greatest joy isn’t how successful some event was. It’s that the boy in her class who could never sit still is now a children’s ministry teacher himself, preparing his lesson every Saturday night. She didn’t teach him any grand principles. She simply showed up in that classroom on time every Lord’s Day, year after year. The faithfulness the children learned was caught by watching.

Faithfulness multiplies in two directions. Upward, you can become the one your pastors and small group leaders can entrust things to without worry. Downward, you can find a younger brother or sister and bring them alongside you in ministry: let them see how you prepare, how you keep time, how you honestly explain when you can’t do something. Don’t only hand them the work; hand them faithfulness too. And the foundation of it all is this: “He who calls you is faithful, who will also do it” (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
lessons.light: The “3” in 235 is the legacy of spiritual parents and children. Legacy doesn’t rest on eloquence; it rests on a reliable life that others can see. When changing a mindset reaches multiplication, faithfulness flows from me to the next generation, making God’s household more stable with each generation.
think: In 2 Timothy 2:1-6, through how many generations does the faith pass, and what pictures does Paul use?
What was my biggest adjustment about faithfulness this week?
Which younger brother or sister can I bring alongside me in ministry?
lessons.speak: Faithful Father, You have called me, and You will also do it. Thank You for teaching me this week to be faithful in small things. Make me someone who can be entrusted with things without worry, and give me a younger brother or sister to walk alongside, so that a faithful life is passed on from generation to generation in Your household. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, invite a younger or newer brother or sister to serve alongside you the next time you serve. Agree on a time beforehand, let them see how you prepare, and pray together afterward.
lessons.quick: What we pass on is not only the work, but a faithful life.
text: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
You therefore must endure hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.
Also, if anyone competes in athletics, he isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules.
The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops.

weeks.title: Gentleness: Restore in a Spirit of Gentleness
weeks.keyText: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
weeks.theme: Gentleness isn’t weakness; it is strength held in check by the Holy Spirit, used to restore people, not to knock them down.
group: Read Galatians 6:1-5. What is the difference between restoring and condemning?
Have you ever been gently restored by someone, or harshly condemned? How did that affect you?
How can we together gently care for a brother or sister who has fallen or drifted away this week?
weeks.sunday: Before Sunday, meditate on Jesus’ words, “I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and ask Him to soften your heart. During the service, notice whom you are criticizing inwardly, and confess it to the Lord. After the service, greet someone you usually don’t see eye to eye with, in a warm and gentle tone.

lessons.title: Restore in Gentleness
lessons.hear:
The church isn’t a club for people without sin; it is a hospital for sinners who have received grace. So Paul speaks very practically: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

The word “restore” was used in that day for mending a torn fishing net, and also for setting a dislocated bone back in place. Setting a bone takes strength, but it takes even more gentleness; push too hard and the bone breaks again. Spiritual people aren’t the ones who stand on the sidelines commenting when someone falls. They are the ones who kneel down and carefully help the person back into place.

Gentleness is often mistaken for weakness or a lack of conviction. But Scripture says, “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3). Moses was anything but weak. He dared to stand before Pharaoh, and he rebuked the people sharply when they worshiped the golden calf. Gentleness isn’t the absence of strength; it is strength held in check by God and used for God—like a well-trained horse whose power is all still there, but which responds to its master’s reins.

Paul adds two more reminders. First, “looking to yourself”: those who restore others must know that they could fall just as easily, and that self-awareness naturally softens their tone. Second, “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2): restoring someone doesn’t end with one conversation; it means walking a stretch of the road with them. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you: when it comes to restoring people, do you need more courage, or more gentleness?
lessons.light: The proud try to restore people by pulling them up from above; the humble come down and help them stand up together. “Looking to yourself” brings us back to our proper place: I need grace just as much as he does. Gentleness is the strength of the selfless life—not to prove that I’m right, but to win my brother.
think: In Galatians 6:1-5, what must those who restore others watch out for in themselves?
When a brother or sister falls, am I more likely to condemn or to avoid?
Is there someone around me who needs to be restored with gentleness?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are gentle and humble in heart; You did not break me, a bruised reed. I confess that when others fall, I often condemn or simply look on. Make me a spiritual person who restores others in a spirit of gentleness, always watching myself, knowing that I need Your mercy just as much. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray for a brother or sister you know is struggling or has fallen, asking the Lord to prepare the right moment. Write down one harsh sentence you want to avoid if you talk with them, and one kind sentence you want to say to them.
lessons.quick: Restoring someone is like setting a bone: it takes strength, and even more gentleness.
text: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.
But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.
For each man will bear his own burden.

lessons.title: The Lord’s Servant Must Not Quarrel
lessons.hear:
In the church’s online group, someone reposted an article about the end times. One brother thought its content was off, so he immediately fired back a long rebuttal with three Bible passages attached, ending with: “Please stop spreading this kind of thing.” The older member who had posted it said nothing more and rarely appeared in the group after that. The brother may have been right about the facts, but he lost a person.

Our old mindset often says that truth matters more than attitude: as long as what I’m saying is right, a harsh tone doesn’t matter. Others swing to the opposite extreme: to keep the peace, they say nothing at all and let error spread. Paul’s instruction to Timothy walks between the two: “The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him” (2 Timothy 2:24-25).

Notice that Paul doesn’t tell Timothy not to teach or not to correct. He tells him to correct “in gentleness.” Why? Because the goal isn’t to win the argument, but that “perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 2:25). It is God who changes hearts, not our volume. Proverbs puts it well: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1).

At the same time, let’s be clear: gentleness doesn’t mean turning a blind eye to error and harm. In cases of spiritual abuse, sexual harassment, violence, or financial misconduct, gentle people will still say a firm “no” and seek help from trusted elders and deacons, the church’s oversight body, or professional services. Those who have been harmed don’t need to stay silent for the sake of peace. Gentleness is about our heart and our manner, not about abandoning truth and justice.
lessons.light: The root of quarreling is the self-centered life: I want to win, I want to be right, I want you to admit it. Selfless gentleness leaves the outcome to God: I do my part to speak the truth, but I don’t have to force the other person to concede right away. Pride provokes pride, and a harsh word stirs up anger; gentleness sets gentleness in motion and turns away wrath.
think: In 2 Timothy 2:24-26, how should the Lord’s servant treat “those who oppose him,” and what is the goal?
In group chats or meetings, am I more likely to argue, or to go silent and avoid it?
Next time we disagree, how will I speak the truth with gentleness?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I often want to win, using the right arguments to say hurtful things; and at other times, afraid of conflict, I don’t speak the truth at all. Give me a gentle heart toward all, able to teach and patient, leaving the work of changing hearts to You. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Recall a recent conversation in a group chat or meeting where your tone was too harsh. Today, privately tell the person, “Last time I spoke too quickly. Please forgive me.” There’s no need to reargue the content.
lessons.quick: Truth must be spoken, but spoken with gentleness; it is God who changes hearts.
text: Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings, knowing that they generate strife.
The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient,
in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,
and they may recover themselves out of the devil’s snare, having been taken captive by him to do his will.

lessons.title: Learn from Him
lessons.hear:
When Jesus describes His own heart in the Gospels, this is what He says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The almighty Son of God introduces Himself with the word “gentle.” His first words to those who labor and are heavily burdened aren’t “What’s wrong with you?” but “Come to me” (Matthew 11:28).

The prophet Isaiah had long foretold this Servant’s gentleness: “He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick” (Isaiah 42:3). The church has many bruised reeds: a sister too ashamed to come to church after her marriage fell apart; a brother who made a mistake in ministry, was removed from his post, and then drifted away; a couple whose child is rebelling and who grow quieter and quieter in small group. What they fear most is being broken again.

Learning from Jesus has some practical details. Listen first; don’t rush to give answers. Ask “Are you okay?” before you ask “Why did you…?” Choose a private setting rather than the group chat or a crowd. Say “we” more and “you” less: “We all need the Lord’s grace.” If the person isn’t ready yet, don’t push; just let them know the door is always open.

Today, find one “bruised reed” and approach them with the gentleness of Jesus. It might be just a message: “Haven’t seen you in a while, and I miss you. No need to reply—I just want you to know I’m praying for you.” It might be a cup of coffee and some time together with no advice attached. Gentleness doesn’t mean saying nothing; it means letting the other person feel accepted first, so they can then hear the truth. Jesus’ yoke is easy because He carries it together with us.
lessons.light: “Learn from me”—Jesus is my example. Gentleness isn’t a natural personality trait; it is a life learned little by little as we share Jesus’ yoke. The “9” of 920 becomes most concrete here: letting a wounded “2” feel the gentle heart of Jesus through me.
think: In Matthew 11:28-30, how does Jesus describe His heart, and whom does He invite?
Does the way I speak sound more like “Come to me” or “What’s wrong with you?”
Which “bruised reed” around me needs me to approach them gently today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, gentle and humble in heart, You did not break me or snuff me out. I am willing to take Your yoke and learn from You. Soften my words and my attitude, and lead me today to a wounded brother or sister, so that they may feel Your heart through me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message with no advice in it to a brother or sister who is struggling or drifting away: “Haven’t seen you in a while, and I miss you. No need to reply—I’m praying for you.” Then pray for them three times this week.
lessons.quick: Let people feel accepted first; then they can hear the truth.
text: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

lessons.title: Moses Strikes the Rock
lessons.hear:
Scripture calls Moses “very humble,” yet even he had a day when he lost control. At Meribah the people quarreled once again because there was no water. God told Moses to take the rod and “speak to the rock before their eyes, that it pour out its water” (Numbers 20:8). Instead Moses said to the assembly, “Hear now, you rebels! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” (Numbers 20:10). Then he raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his rod.

The water still came out; God still provided for His people. But God said to Moses, “Because you didn’t believe in me, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel” (Numbers 20:12). The problem wasn’t only his temper. In his anger, Moses had put the spotlight on himself—“Shall we bring water… for you?”—forgetting that he was only a servant. We often lose our gentleness because we have quietly stepped into God’s place.

This is a mirror every leader should look into. A man who had led a small group for many years finally snapped one evening when, yet again, people arrived late and others scrolled on their phones. He said coldly, “If you don’t want to come, you don’t have to.” The meeting was very quiet that night, and afterward two people really did stop coming. He made his point, but people got hurt. Accumulated fatigue, the feeling of being let down, disappointment with “these people”—any of these can make a gentle person suddenly raise the rod and strike the rock.

The good news is that Moses’ story doesn’t end in failure. Centuries later, on the mountain of the Transfiguration, Moses appeared with Elijah and talked with Jesus (see Matthew 17:1-3). The way to adjust is this: admit your anger, and don’t justify it with “I was doing it for their good.” Apologize to those you hurt. Return to God and draw on His gentleness again. And be honest about your own exhaustion—sometimes restoring gentleness takes rest, and it takes co-workers who will share the load.
lessons.light: “Shall we bring water… for you?” Those words expose the self-centered life: ministry has become my achievement, and the people’s weakness has become my burden. The selfless know that the water comes from God, not from me. When we return to our proper place as servants, anger loses its root, and gentleness grows back.
think: In Numbers 20:7-12, how did God’s instructions differ from what Moses did?
Recently, in serving or leading, have I had a “striking the rock” moment?
Whom do I need to apologize to, and where do I need to ask others to share the load so I can rest?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I too have struck the rock: in exhaustion and disappointment I have wounded Your sheep with harsh words, and told myself it was for their good. Forgive me for stepping into Your place. Bring me back to my proper place as a servant, let me draw on Your gentleness again, and teach me to ask You and my co-workers for help when I am weary. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a time in ministry when you lost your gentleness and spoke harshly. Today, apologize to that person or group. If you are feeling worn out, tell your small group leader or pastor and ask for help sharing the load.
lessons.quick: I often lose my gentleness because I’ve quietly stepped into God’s place.
text: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

“Take the rod, and assemble the congregation, you, and Aaron your brother, and speak to the rock before their eyes, that it pour out its water. You shall bring water to them out of the rock; so you shall give the congregation and their livestock drink.”
Moses took the rod from before the LORD, as he commanded him.
Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly together before the rock, and he said to them, “Hear now, you rebels! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?”
Moses lifted up his hand, and struck the rock with his rod twice, and water came out abundantly. The congregation and their livestock drank.

The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Because you didn’t believe in me, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land which I have given them.”

lessons.title: Answer with Humility and Fear
lessons.hear:
The man who wrote this passage was Peter—the one who once drew his sword in the garden and cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant (see John 18:10). The impulsive fisherman had been changed by the gentle heart of Jesus. He writes, “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear” (1 Peter 3:15). The word rendered “humility” here is the same word translated “gentleness” in the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23).

This week we have seen gentleness in different forms. It is the hand that sets a bone, restoring the fallen to their place. It is the gentle mouth that speaks the truth in disagreement without quarreling. It is the gentle heart of Jesus, which does not break a bruised reed. And it is the mirror of Moses, reminding us that when we lose our gentleness, it is often because we are standing in the wrong place. The root of gentleness is to “sanctify the Lord God in your hearts”: when Christ reigns in my heart, I no longer need to protect myself by being hard.

The first place gentleness is passed on is the home. Children mostly learn their tone of voice from their parents; new believers mostly learn how to handle disagreement by watching their small group leader. Paul reminds us “to speak evil of no one, not to be contentious, to be gentle, showing all humility toward all men” (Titus 3:2). Gentleness is something that can be seen and imitated.

The assignment for multiplication is to find a setting where you can model gentleness. Perhaps you can help a young small group leader prepare for a difficult conversation, teaching them to listen first, then ask, then speak. Perhaps at a youth gathering you can share how a gentle word once restored you. Jesus said, “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). The gentle don’t gain the land by seizing it; they inherit it, generation after generation, through God’s promise.
lessons.light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Gentleness is the fruit of life; it produces healthy relationships, and only then beautiful ministry. Spiritual parents in 235 don’t only pass on knowledge; they pass on tone and attitude. The next generation will treat the generation after them the way we treat them.
think: In 1 Peter 3:14-16, what must be in our hearts before we answer anyone?
This week, in what situation did I experience the change gentleness brings?
In front of whom will I model gentleness—my children, my small group members, or newcomers?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You changed impulsive Peter into a gentle shepherd; please change me the same way. Be sanctified as Lord in my heart, so that I no longer need to protect myself by being hard. Let my family, my small group members, and the next generation learn gentleness from me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
