lessons.do: Today, find a young person or child you are walking alongside and share a time you were restored by gentleness. Then ask them, “Is there a relationship right now that we could face together with gentleness?”
lessons.quick: When Christ is sanctified as Lord in my heart, I don’t need hardness to protect myself.
text: But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. “Don’t fear what they fear, neither be troubled.”
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,
having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.

weeks.title: Self-Control: Swift to Hear, Slow to Speak
weeks.keyText: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
weeks.theme: Self-control is letting the Holy Spirit govern my tongue, emotions, and desires; a single sentence can build up a church or tear it down.
group: Read James 1:19-27. Of “swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger,” which is hardest for you?
Have you ever been hurt by a word in church or a group chat, or hurt someone else? What did that teach you?
Could our small group agree on one guideline for how we speak, to remind each other this week—for example, not forwarding unverified news?
weeks.sunday: Before Sunday, pray: “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” (Psalm 141:3). During the service, listen more and critique less; notice the criticisms that rise in your heart and hand them to the Lord. After the service, in casual conversation, speak only words that build others up, and give specific encouragement to one ministry team member who served.

lessons.title: Swift to Hear, Slow to Speak
lessons.hear:
The letter of James is often called the Proverbs of the New Testament—short, sharp, and piercing. He tells the church, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:19-20). Three speeds: quick to listen, slow to speak, and slower still to get angry. Yet we so often have it exactly backwards: slow to listen, quick to speak, and quicker still to get angry.

Self-control is the last of the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit, and it works like a levee that protects the other eight. Without self-control, passion turns into indulgence, frankness into harshness, and zeal into impatience. The original word carries the idea of “having mastery over oneself.” Proverbs says, “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32). The truly strong person isn’t the one who can control others, but the one governed by the Holy Spirit and therefore able to rule his own heart.

James ties self-control especially to the tongue: “If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless” (James 1:26). A person can be very zealous, very knowledgeable, very good at praying—but if he can’t control his mouth, his religion is like a tire with a slow leak. It looks fine from the outside, but it won’t take him far.

But remember: self-control isn’t self-improvement by gritting your teeth. It is the fruit of the Spirit. James tells us to “receive with humility the implanted word” (James 1:21). When God’s word takes root in our hearts, the Holy Spirit becomes a new set of brakes within us. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you: of these three—listening, speaking, and anger—which speed most needs adjusting in you?
lessons.light: Self-centered people speak quickly, because they are eager to express and prove themselves. Selfless people listen quickly, because their hearts have room for others. Rely on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head: before you open your mouth, let the Spirit who lives in you filter your words.
think: In James 1:19-27, what situations of “deceiving yourself” does James mention?
Of the three speeds—listening, speaking, and anger—which do I most need to adjust?
In what setting today will I make a point of listening more and speaking less?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, please produce the fruit of self-control in me. I confess that I am often slow to listen, quick to speak, and even quicker to get angry. Bridle my tongue, help me receive Your word with humility, and filter my words before I speak, so that what I say no longer serves my anger but works the righteousness of God. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in one conversation (with family, a ministry team member, or a small group member), deliberately let the other person finish speaking, then restate what they meant in one sentence before you respond. In the evening, write down what difference this made.
lessons.quick: Quick to listen, slow to speak, slower still to anger.
text: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.
If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless.
Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.

lessons.title: A Small Rudder, a Spreading Fire
lessons.hear:
At eleven o’clock one night, a voice message popped up in the church ministry team’s group chat. A brother in charge of the facilities, angry that no one had cleaned up after an event, spoke for two minutes and called out three team members by name. The next day, once he had calmed down, he sent a line: “I was too tired last night. Sorry.” But those two minutes had already been played more than twenty times, and one of the young team members he named quietly stepped away from ministry.

We often make excuses for our mouths: “I’m just a straight shooter,” “I’m only telling the truth,” “I was just talking—it’s no big deal.” But James gives us two pictures: “Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires” (James 3:4). The tongue is small, yet it decides where a whole ship—a small group, a team, a church—will go. He goes on: “And the tongue is a fire” (James 3:6). One sentence can warm someone, or burn down trust that took years to build.

The sentence that stings the most is this: “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God. Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not” (James 3:9-10). On Sunday morning we sing praises loudly in the choir, and on the drive home we criticize the sermon and the ministry team. In the group chat we repost Bible verses, and in private messages we talk about a brother or sister behind their back. The same mouth pours out both sweet and bitter water.

God’s perspective is this: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21). Words are never “just talk”; they carry power. In the online age that power is magnified: a single sentence can be screenshotted, forwarded, and kept for years. So a self-controlled tongue isn’t timid—it is reverent. I know my words are spoken before God, and that they will land on a person made in the image of God.
lessons.light: “I’m just a straight shooter” is often the packaging of the self-centered life: my feelings must be expressed immediately, and I’m not responsible for anyone else’s. Selfless people think first of the “2” who will hear their words. Proud words provoke pride; self-controlled words bring peace. Only when we hand the tongue’s rudder to the Holy Spirit will the church’s ship sail steadily.
think: What pictures does James 3:1-10 use to describe the tongue?
Do I often use “I’m just being honest” to excuse what I say?
Is there something I’ve said that I need to go back and clean up or apologize for?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that my mouth often pours out both sweet and bitter water: praising You in the gathering, then turning around and criticizing the people You love. Forgive me for treating the power of words lightly, as if it were “just talk.” Holy Spirit, take charge of my tongue, so that my words become life, not fire. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Recall something you recently said about a brother or sister in a group chat, private message, or conversation. Today, stop passing it along and confess it to the Lord. If the person has already been affected, privately apologize to them.
lessons.quick: The tongue is a rudder and a fire; think of the listener before you speak.
text: Let not many of you be teachers, my brothers, knowing that we will receive heavier judgment.
For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.
Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body.
Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.
So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!
And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind;
but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.

lessons.title: Three Seconds Before You Hit Send
lessons.hear:
Paul reminds the church in Colossae, “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:6). In the ancient world, salt both flavored food and kept it from spoiling. Words seasoned with salt are easy for people to take in, and they keep relationships from going bad. Notice that this passage begins with “Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving” (Colossians 4:2): only a heart soaked in prayer can speak words seasoned with salt.

Today’s practice is this: every time before you speak or hit “send,” give yourself three seconds and ask three questions. First, is it true? Unverified news and secondhand stories don’t get passed along. Second, will it build others up? Paul says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). Third, is this the right time and place? Things that should be discussed privately don’t go in the group chat; when emotions are at their peak, don’t hit send yet.

Self-control doesn’t only govern the tongue; it also governs emotions and desires. The urge to cut in and win the argument at a ministry team meeting; the sour impulse to add a comment when someone else is praised; the heart that grabs the best dishes first at the church potluck and rushes out the moment the meeting ends—these are all places that need the Holy Spirit’s restraint. Paul says, “Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things” (1 Corinthians 9:25), and we do it for an incorruptible crown.

The method can be very simple. Set this prayer from the Psalms as your phone wallpaper: “Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.” (Psalm 141:3). Read it once before posting in a group chat. When emotions rise, put the phone down, take a walk, pray for five minutes, and then decide whether to reply. You’ll find that many things don’t need to be said once three seconds have passed—and the things that truly need saying will be said better after prayer.
lessons.light: Rely on the Spirit with your heart: a three-second pause is the space where we hand authority back to the Holy Spirit. Letting Jesus reign isn’t only for life’s big decisions, but for every message and every comment. Self-controlled speech is the fruit of the “9” in 920 that is most visible in the online world.
think: In Colossians 4:2-6, what spiritual disciplines does Paul connect with our speech?
In online group chats, what speech mistake do I make most often?
What specific method will I use to remind myself to pause three seconds before I hit send?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, set a guard over my mouth, and take charge of the keyboard in my hands too. Before I speak or send a message, help me stop and ask You: Is it true? Will it build up? Is it the right time? Holy Spirit, restrain my emotions and desires, so that my speech is always with grace, seasoned with salt. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, set a reminder or wallpaper on your phone: “True? Building up? Right time?” Put it into practice before posting in your church group chat. In the evening, count how many messages you rewrote or didn’t send because of it.
lessons.quick: Pause three seconds before you send: Is it true? Will it build up? Is it the right time?
text: Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving,
praying together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds,
that I may reveal it as I ought to speak.
Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time.
Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

lessons.title: Peter Draws His Sword
lessons.hear:
Peter is one of the least self-controlled disciples in the New Testament. He blurted out, “Even if all will be made to stumble because of you, I will never be made to stumble” (Matthew 26:33). In the garden, on impulse, he drew his sword: “Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it, struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear” (John 18:10). A few hours later, the same mouth said to a servant girl at the door, “I am not” (John 18:17).

Impulsiveness and cowardice look like opposites, but they share the same root: both are being dragged along by the emotion of the moment. Drawing the sword was driven by anger and hot blood; the denial was driven by fear. A person without self-control doesn’t only say too much; he also often goes silent when he should speak and backs down when he should stand firm. It’s the same in church: some pound the table at ministry team meetings, while others say nothing when a problem surfaces, then complain about it in private afterward. Neither is governed by the Holy Spirit.

Take time to review. When was the last time I “drew my sword”—in a meeting, in a group chat, or at home? And when was the last time I “denied”? When I should have spoken up for the truth or for someone being mistreated, did I stay silent because I was afraid of offending people? Proverbs says, “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint” (Proverbs 25:28).

But Peter’s story is a story of restoration. Jesus didn’t give up on him; after the resurrection He asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (see John 21:15-17). On the day of Pentecost, Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, stood up and preached, and the same mouth became an instrument for building the church (see Acts 2:14). Years later he wrote to the churches, “But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer” (1 Peter 4:7). Self-control doesn’t come from gritting our teeth; it is the fruit that grows naturally once we are restored by the Lord’s love and filled with the Holy Spirit.
lessons.light: When emotions reign, the self reigns; whether it is anger or fear, both are grabbing for Jesus’ place. The way to adjust isn’t to push down harder, but to be filled with the Holy Spirit. The restored Peter no longer drew his sword, nor did he deny; he spoke when it was time to speak and was quiet when it was time to be quiet.
think: In John 18:10-18, what emotion drove each of Peter’s two reactions?
Am I more prone to “draw my sword” or to “deny”? When was the last time?
How can I let the Holy Spirit govern my emotions more fully?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You didn’t give up on impulsive, weak Peter, and You haven’t given up on me. I confess that sometimes anger pushes me to draw my sword, and sometimes fear pushes me into silence. Holy Spirit, fill me and rule my heart, so that I speak when it is time to speak and keep quiet when it is time to be quiet, and become an instrument for building Your church. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down a recent time you “drew your sword” and a time you “denied,” and for each write one sentence about how you will do it differently. If needed, apologize to a brother or sister hurt by your impulsive words.
lessons.quick: Anger and fear both want to reign; only when filled with the Spirit can I rule my own heart.
text: Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it, struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.
Jesus therefore said to Peter, “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?”
So the detachment, the commanding officer, and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him,
and led him to Annas first, for he was father-in-law to Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.
Now it was Caiaphas who advised the Jews that it was expedient that one man should perish for the people.
Simon Peter followed Jesus, as did another disciple. Now that disciple was known to the high priest, and entered in with Jesus into the court of the high priest;
but Peter was standing at the door outside. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to her who kept the door, and brought in Peter.
Then the maid who kept the door said to Peter, “Are you also one of this man’s disciples?” He said, “I am not.”
Now the servants and the officers were standing there, having made a fire of coals, for it was cold. They were warming themselves. Peter was with them, standing and warming himself.

lessons.title: One Fruit, Nine Flavors
lessons.hear:
For these nine weeks, we have walked through the fruit of the Spirit one fruit at a time. Today we return to the starting point: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23). Notice that Paul says “fruit,” singular. The nine aren’t nine items on a performance review; they are nine flavors of the one life of Christ—like a ripe piece of fruit that has color, fragrance, and taste all at once.

A brief look back over the journey: love is the root that makes us patient with imperfect brothers and sisters; joy lets us rejoice with those who rejoice; peace makes us eager to pursue harmony; patience lets us bear with one another in love; kindness moves us to show grace to the undeserving; goodness puts love into action; faithfulness makes us reliable in small things; gentleness is used to restore those who have fallen; and self-control guards the tongue, so that all the fruit before it isn’t ruined by a single sentence.

The secret of it all is in the next two verses: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts. If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:24-25). This is the selfless “0”: the old self is nailed to the cross, so the life of Christ can grow in me. Paul then adds, “Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another” (Galatians 5:26). Fruit isn’t for comparing; it’s for feeding others.

This brings the “life” stage to a close. Our mindset has changed, and now that life must go on to change our living, our relationships, and our ministry. The assignment for multiplication is to sit down with a companion or your small group and review the nine-fold fruit together. Tell each other one fruit you have seen in the other person, and name the one area where you most need the Holy Spirit to bear fruit in you. You will find that the best mirror is your brothers and sisters, and the best garden is a group of people being cultivated together by the Holy Spirit.
lessons.light: The complete picture of 920: in every relationship with the “2,” practice the selfless “0,” and bear the “9”—the fruit of Christ’s life. We don’t cultivate nine virtues by our own effort; when we let Jesus reign and let the Holy Spirit guide, the fruit grows naturally. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the fruit of life is the foundation of all the service that follows.
think: In Galatians 5:22-26, what are the conditions for bearing fruit?
Over these nine weeks, in which fruit have I grown the most, and which do I need most?
With whom will I review the fruit, telling each other the fruit we see in one another?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, thank You for Your work in me over these nine weeks. Once again I lay my old self on the cross; I want to live by You and walk by You. Bear the life of Christ in my relationship with every brother and sister, so that people may taste in me Your love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, meet with your spiritual companion or small group and read Galatians 5:22-26 together. Have each person name one fruit they see in someone else and one fruit they most need themselves, then pray for one another.
lessons.quick: Nine flavors, one life—Christ living in me.
